passages.text: Vascular calcification (VC) is an active process akin to bone formation and results not only from an elevation in calcium/phosphorus serum levels but also from the dysregulated induction of osteogenesis. The differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells into osteoblast-like cells results in a bone matrix synthesis. Then, the loss of mineralization inhibitors, which could be estimated using the calcification propensity score, leads to VCs. Active inducers of VC in CKD mainly include accumulation of uremic toxins, mineral disorders (such as hypercalcemia, high inorganic phosphate and intact parathyroid hormone [iPTH] levels, low vitamin D3, fibroblast growth factor-23 [FGF-23]), and inflammation. Among mineralization inhibitors, pyrophosphates, alpha-Klotho, and active matrix gla protein (MGP) are the most studied molecules. Of note, systems controlling bone metabolism including Wnt signaling pathway inhibitors such as sclerostin (SOST) and the osteoprotegerin (OPG)/RANK/RANK ligand complex also constitute regulators of central significance in VC.

infons.name: Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder

passages.text: Interestingly, growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) superfamily, constitutes another molecule of interest. Indeed, correlations of GDF-15 with CV and non-CV mortality have been documented, and a primary role in multiple CV diseases, including heart failure, cardiac hypertrophy, and coronary heart disease, has been ascribed to it. Regarding its implication in VC, only indirect evidence is currently available with experimental studies reporting promotion of osteoclast and inhibition of osteoblast differentiation. Therefore, the present study aimed to explore the potential additive values of a detrimental environment (combining a micro-inflammatory state, disturbances in mineral metabolism, and arterial calcifications) on major adverse CV events (MACE)/CV mortality in a prospective cohort of non-dialysis CKD (ND-CKD) patients in order to develop targeted therapies.
Methods
Ethics Statement

The study was conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and in compliance with International Conference on Harmonization/Good Clinical Practice regulations. According to the French Law, this study (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT00608998 and NCT02808572) has been registered at "Ministere de la Sante et des Solidarites" after approval by the Nimes University Hospital's Ethics Committee. All patients gave their written informed consent.
Subjects

ND-CKD patients at various stages of kidney disease, issued from the outpatient general nephrology consultation of the Montpellier Lapeyronie university hospital, were enrolled in this prospective observational study. Inclusion criteria were age >=18 years and the presence of CKD defined, in agreement with the National Kidney Foundation, as either kidney damage or glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for >=3 months. Kidney damage was defined as pathologic abnormalities or markers of damage, including abnormalities in blood or urine tests or imaging studies. Detailed medical history including age, gender, weight, height, cause of CKD, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, past or current smoking, the presence of CV disease was recorded (see the online suppl. Materials; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000542418).
Procedures
Laboratory Measurements

At inclusion, blood samples were collected as part of our regular CKD patient management plan, centrifuged, and supernatant was stored at -80 C until measurement of the following parameters: creatinine, calcium, phosphate, 25(OH) vitamin D3, iPTH, albumin, high-sensitive C reactive protein (hsCRP), bone ALP, dephosphorylated uncarboxylated (dp-uc) MGP, total uncarboxylated (t-uc) MGP, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b (TRAP5b), OPG, SOST, FGF-23, alpha-Klotho, and GDF-15. Assays were sequentially done with less than 1-year intervals after freezing.

Evaluation of routine biological parameters including creatinine, calcium, phosphate, 25(OH) vitamin D3, iPTH, albumin, and hsCRP was performed on a cobas 8000 analyzer (Roche, Meylan, France). The GFR was estimated using the CKD-EPI equation. Bone ALP, dp-ucMGP, t-ucMGP, and TRAP5b were assessed using automated IDS-iSYS methods (Immunodiagnostic Systems, Boldon, UK). OPG, SOST, FGF-23 (both intact and C-terminal fragments), and alpha-Klotho were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (OPG: Biovendor Laboratory Medicine, Brno, Czech Republic; SOST: TECOmedical Quidel Corporation, San Diego, CA, USA; FGF-23: Immutopics International Inc, San Clemente, CA, USA; soluble alpha-Klotho: IBL, Minneapolis, MN, USA). GDF-15 was measured by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (Elecsys GDF-15, Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim) on a cobas analyzer.
Coronary Artery Calcification Imaging

At inclusion, patients underwent multidetector computed tomography. Regarding data acquisition, all multidetector computed tomography scans derived from a multidetector-row spiral CT (Lightspeed VCT, General Electric Medical System, Milwaukee, WI, USA). Prospective ECG-triggered step-scan was performed using with 2.5-mm collimation width x64 detectors so that the center of the temporal window corresponded to 70% of the R-R interval. The scanning parameters were a gantry rotation speed of 0.35 s/rotation, 120 kV, and 300 mA 8X2.5 collimation and 20 mm table feed per rotation. The matrix size was 512 x 512 pixels, and the display field of view was 25 cm. The reconstruction kernel was standard. The temporal resolution was 250 ms.

Regarding image evaluation, the calcium score was calculated using a semiautomatic software (Smartscore version 3.5, Advantage Window 4.4 workstation, General Electric, Milwaukee, WI, USA). Coronary calcification was defined as a plaque of >=4 pixels (area = 1.37 mm2) with a density of >=130 Hounsfield units. Quantitative calcium scores were calculated according to the method described by Agatston et al.. Coronary calcium scoring was performed by either a physician or computed tomography technician with specific training for the methodology described above. The presence of severe coronary artery calcification (CAC) was defined by a CAC >=300 and an insignificant or moderate CAC by a CAC <300.
Follow-Up and Clinical Outcomes

Patients were included between 2004 and 2018 and were followed up to the first MACE, CV death, transplantation, dialysis initiation or were censored at 26th April 2018, whichever came first. Deaths were recorded using medical charts. Components of MACE included acute coronary syndrome or ischemic heart disease; coronary revascularization procedures (angioplasty or bypass grafting); valvular cardiopathy if decompensation; heart failure; acute pulmonary edema; stroke (either ischemic or hemorrhagic); transient ischemic attack; arteriopathy of the lower limb (above stage II); lower limb, aorta, or renal artery revascularization procedures.
Statistical Methods

Characteristics of the population were described by using proportions for categorical variables and means and standard deviation for quantitative variables. Biological parameters were divided into tertiles.

Proportional hazard Cox models were performed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and their confidence intervals (CIs) for studying the associations between baseline biological parameters (considered as both categorical and continuous variables) and the risk of MACE/CV mortality. In the case of multiple events during the follow-up period, only the first event was considered in the survival analysis. Proportional hazards assumption was tested using the Schoenfeld residuals. Three models were successively performed: without adjustment (model 0); adjustment for age and gender (model 1); adjustment for age, gender, diabetes, and history of CV events (model 2).

To determine whether CAC and CV risk biomarkers were independently associated with MACE/CV mortality, all variables were simultaneously entered into a stepwise proportional hazard Cox model with potential confounders: gender, age, CV history, diabetes, smoker status, body mass index associated with MACE/CV mortality at p < 0.10. The best fitting model was selected using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).

To investigate potential additive effects of biological variables and CAC on MACE/CV mortality occurrence, composite indexes were created, categorizing patients based on high levels of CAC and either low or high levels of iPTH, hsCRP, 25(OH) vitamin D3, FGF-23, alpha-Klotho, OPG, SOST, dp-ucMGP, and GDF-15. The cutoffs of variables were chosen as tertiles values strongly associated with MACE/CV mortality. The associations between these composite indexes and the risk of MACE/CV mortality were described using the Kaplan-Meier method and tested for statistical significance using the log-rank test.

Logistic regression models were performed to estimate odds ratio and their 95% CI for studying the associations between CAC extent and vascular risk biomarkers. The significance level was set a p < 0.05. All analyses were carried out with SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).
Results
Patient Characteristics

Four hundred and twenty-five patients were included in the study. Table 1 depicts their clinical and biological characteristics at inclusion. Among the 425 patients, 152 (35.8%) patients had severe CAC (score >= 300).

Causes of CKD were glomerulonephritis (n = 65), autosomal polycystic kidney disease (n = 38), diabetic kidney disease (n = 40), diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy (n = 40), angiosclerosis and hypertensive nephropathy (n = 131), infectious/obstructive interstitial nephropathy (n = 16), nephrectomy following renal neoplasia (n = 4), genetic/congenital cause (n = 4), necrotizing angiitis (n = 7), unknown cause (n = 27), other cause (n = 53).
Occurrence of MACE according to CV Markers

During the follow-up (median time of 3.61 years [25th-75th percentiles = 1.92-6.70]), MACE/CV mortality occurred in 69 patients (55 [79.7%] were men): acute coronary syndrome or ischemic heart disease (myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stress testing or dobutamine positive test) (n = 14), coronary revascularization procedures (angioplasty or bypass grafting) (n = 6), valvular cardiopathy if decompensation (n = 3), heart failure and acute pulmonary edema (n = 8), stroke (either ischemic or hemorrhagic) or transient ischemic attack (n = 10), arteriopathy of the lower limb (above stage II) (n = 9), lower limb revascularization procedures (n = 10), aorta or renal artery revascularization procedures (n = 6), CV death (n = 3). The risk of MACE events or CV death increased in older patients (HR = 1.04, 95% CI = [1.01-1.06], p = 0.0003), male (HR = 2.75, 95% CI = [1.53-4.95], p = 0.0007), with diabetes mellitus (HR = 3.34, 95% CI = [2.07-5.38], p < 0.0001), history of CV events (HR = 3.34, 95% CI = [1.93-5.79], p < 0.0001), and a lower estimated GFR (HR = 1.02, 95% CI = [1.00-1.03], p = 0.01).

The relationships between the presence of CAC, biological parameters, and MACE/CV death occurrence are presented in Table 2 (parameters being considered as tertiles). Only high levels of CAC, hsCRP, and iPTH were associated with a higher MACE/CV mortality occurrence (in both unadjusted analysis [model 0] and after adjustments for age and gender [model 1]). However, when diabetes and history of CV events confounders were entered in the model (model 2), only iPTH remained associated with MACE/CV mortality. Significant associations were observed between high levels of SOST or GDF-15 and high occurrence of MACE/CV mortality in the unadjusted analysis, but they did not reach significance after adjustments. Using continuous variables, CAC, hsCRP, and iPTH were significantly associated with MACE/CV mortality whatever the adjustment was (see online suppl. Table 1).

Discussion

This study aimed at analyzing the predictive values of CAC and biomarkers of CV risk on MACE/CV mortality in a sample of 425 ND-CKD patients. Our findings indicate that CAC stands out as a significant independent factor for MACE/CV mortality, exhibiting a HR comparable to that of diabetes, history of CV events, iPTH, and hsCRP. Furthermore, the predictive efficacy of CAC was notably heightened in conjunction with elevated levels of hsCRP, iPTH, FGF-23, dp-ucMGP, OPG, SOST, GDF-15 and diminished levels of 25(OH) vitamin D3 and alpha-Klotho.

When analyzing the predictive value of all biomarkers on MACE/mortality occurrence, only hsCRP and iPTH were strongly independently associated with MACE/CV mortality after adjustment for age and gender; all other biomarkers of CV risk not being predictive per se of adverse events. Interestingly, the presence of an inflammatory environment, hyperparathyroidism, and bone remodeling molecules involved in CV risk (including high FGF-23, OPG, SOST, dp-ucMGP, and GDF-15 along with low 25(OH) vitamin D3 and alpha-Klotho) dramatically worsened the predictive value of CAC after full adjustment (model 2). Thus, one can hypothesize that VC conspire with inflammation, hyperparathyroidism and factors of bone/vascular calcification remodeling to promote MACE/CV mortality.

The role of VC in atherosclerosis and subsequent poor outcome remains a matter of ongoing controversy, being recognized as either protective or deleterious. Some studies have reported that calcified plaques are more stable than non-calcified plaques. Conversely, others could evidence that calcified plaques independently predict combined vascular events. Several factors may explain such contradictory findings, including the phenotype of the calcification and the surrounding environment which may exert differential roles in plaque homeostasis. Microcalcifications and spotty calcifications may represent an active stage of VC correlated with inflammation and may increase the risk of plaque rupture in the fibrous plaque. By contrast, macrocalcifications would contain rather reparative macrophages including osteoclast-like cells and fewer inflammatory cells and would be a typical feature of more stable plaques and asymptomatic disease. Of note, both types of calcifications can coexist during plaque progression. In CKD, two main uremia-related pathways may simultaneously contribute to the risk of MACE: ongoing VC remodeling leading to spotty calcifications and inflammatory process within established plaques. Our results align with this hypothesis. First, the increased risk of MACE associated with the combination of VC turnover biomarkers and CAC highlights the detrimental implication of coronary artery remodeling. Numerous studies have demonstrated the involvement of procalcifying agents such as FGF-23, OPG, SOST, and dp-ucMGP, the inactive form of MGP and their potential synergistic effects on VC. Our results (see online suppl. Table 3) corroborate the association of CAC with vascular bone remodeling factors and suggest that elevated levels of FGF-23, SOST, OPG, and dp-ucMGP worsen CAC prognosis (Fig. 1 and online suppl. Table 2). Interestingly, unfunctional MGP has been shown to facilitate initial calcium crystal deposition and early nidus formation. In addition, GDF-15 emerged as another biomarker strongly associated with CAC and MACE. GDF-15, a stress-inducible cytokine upregulated by several inflammatory or stress-related proteins, exhibits a paradoxical and controversial role in CV diseases. Indeed, studies in animal models suggest that GDF-15 may prevent or reduce plaque formation. Conversely, clinical studies indicate that high GDF-15 levels are associated with heart failure and with the severity of CAC in both the general population and male patients with end stage kidney disease. Notably, Mayer et al. recently demonstrated that stable coronary heart disease patients with high levels of both GDF-15 and dp-ucMGP faced an increased risk of MACE. In the same manner, the inverse relationship between vitamin D or alpha-Klotho and CAC has been previously documented. Our findings confirm these data and clearly demonstrate that high levels of 25(OH) vitamin D3 or alpha-Klotho protect against MACE (Fig. 1 and online suppl. Table 2). The protective effect of circulating alpha-Klotho aligns with its beneficial role in VC and heart disease observed in animal models using recombinant Klotho.

The surrounding inflammatory environment may also substantially contribute to the risk of MACE associated with severe CAC. A highly pro-inflammatory milieu can promote the recruitment and activation of neutrophils, leading to SMC death via neutrophil extracellular traps and subsequent necrotic core enlargement. The enrichment of inflammatory cells and the expansion of the necrotic core can increase plaque instability and ultimately lead to plaque rupture.

Interestingly, as recently well described, macrophages, the main inflammatory cells involved in atherosclerotic plaques, can exert a dual role in the disease progression, due to their remarkable plasticity and functional heterogeneity. Originally, two subpopulations have been defined: classically activated (M1-like phenotype) and alternatively activated (M2-like phenotype) macrophages with respective pro- and anti-inflammatory properties. M1 macrophages produce pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, etc.) that promote the differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells into osteoblasts and stimulate the production of reactive oxygen species and bone morphogenetic proteins. M2 macrophages, in turn, present different properties, sometimes opposite, to M1 macrophages. They secrete anti-inflammatory factors (including IL-10) that help reduce the inflammation by inhibiting the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and by reducing the production of reactive oxygen species. M1 macrophages are associated with unstable plaques, while M2 macrophages are more common in asymptomatic lesions and in stable zones of plaques. M1 polarization is dependent on inflammatory conditions. The preferential M1- or M2-like phenotyping shift may also be dependent on the calcified milieu as calcium phosphate supplementation can promote M1 polarization. Results of our study clearly demonstrated that inflammation and hyperparathyroidism could drive a shift toward a pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype, worsening the prognostic value of CAC for CV events (Fig. 2).

Hypotheses on mechanism of action macrophages can exert a dual role in the disease progression, due to their remarkable plasticity and functional heterogeneity. Originally, two subpopulations were defined: classically activated (M1-like phenotype) and alternatively activated (M2-like phenotype) macrophages with, respectively, pro- and anti-inflammatory properties. M1 macrophages are associated with unstable plaques, while M2 macrophages are more common in asymptomatic lesions and in stable zones of plaques. M1 polarization is dependent on inflammatory conditions. Results of our study suggest that inflammation and hyperparathyroidism could be responsible for a shift toward pro-inflammatory M1-like and worsened the prognostic value of CAC in CV events.

Of note, the M1-M2 polarization and vascular-bone remodeling pathways are closely interconnected. In osteosarcoma biopsies, a positive correlation between M1-polarized macrophages and OPG expression has been observed. This relationship between OPG, as a surrogate of OPG/RANK/RANKL pathway dysregulation, and the M1 phenotype aligns with our previous findings showing that OPG levels predict poor outcomes in hemodialysis patients, but only in an inflammatory context. Similarly, the interplay between bone remodeling factors (SOST and RANKL) and macrophage polarization has been demonstrated during alveolar bone repair. On the other hand, previous studies have evidenced that active vitamin D can downregulate macrophage transition to the M1 phenotype. Similarly, alpha-Klotho has been shown to promote microglial polarization toward the M2 phenotype, which may exhibit anti-inflammatory properties. It could be assumed that the effect of alpha-Klotho on M2 polarization in microglia could also apply to macrophages. All these findings are consistent with our results reporting a poor outcome in patients with deficient levels of 25(OH) vitamin D3 and low levels of circulating alpha-Klotho. Additional anti-inflammatory properties of vitamin D and alpha-Klotho may also be highlighted in this population. In summary, the original findings of this study aimed to introduce the concept of "multiple hits" contributing to the occurrence of MACE in patients with CKD.

Our study acknowledges certain limitations. First, being a single-center study, there may be limitations in generalizability. Additionally, an extended follow-up duration could have strengthened the observed relationships between biomarkers and MACE/CV mortality. The inclusion of a broader array of biomarkers, such as pro/anti-inflammatory cytokines, could have further validated the involvement of inflammatory processes in the occurrence of MACE/CV mortality. In addition, some parameters including 25(OH) vitamin D3 and dc-ucMGP could not be measured in the entire patient population. Lastly, a qualitative exploration of plaques would have yielded supplementary information, enhancing the understanding of the assumptions made regarding the nature of calcifications.
Conclusion

In conclusion, our findings emphasize that the adverse prognosis associated with CAC in CKD is exacerbated by a detrimental environment, encompassing inflammation or surrogate biomarkers indicative of active bone matrix synthesis or mineralization, such as iPTH, FGF-23, OPG, and SOST. Conversely, vitamin D and alpha-Klotho may offer protective effects on CAC-related poor outcomes, potentially through mechanisms involving M2 macrophage polarization or anti-inflammatory pathways. This study introduces the original concept of "multiple hits" contributing to the occurrence of MACE. Consequently, effective therapeutic strategies aimed at improving CV outcomes in CKD patients should focus on mitigating the harmful environment that fosters plaque vulnerability, curtailing chronic microinflammation, and normalizing mineral metabolism and vascular bone remodeling.

passages.text: Glycosphingolipids and their impact on platelet activity in a murine model of fabry disease

Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme  -galactosidase-A ( -Gal A), resulting in widespread accumulation of terminal galactose-containing glycosphingolipids (GSLs) and the impairment of multiple organ systems. Thrombotic events are common in Fabry patients, with strokes and heart attacks being significant contributors to a shortened lifespan in patients of both genders. Previously, we developed an  -Gal A-knockout (KO) murine model that recapitulates most Fabry symptomologies and demonstrated that platelets from KO males become sensitized to agonist-mediated activation. In the current report, we used mass spectrometry, platelet-based assays and histology to define further the mechanisms linking GSL accumulation with thrombotic phenotypes in both sexes. Sera and platelets from  -Gal A-KO females have elevated levels of Fabry-associated GSLs relative to wild-type females, but accumulated less of these GSLs than KO males. Correspondingly, KO females demonstrate a less severe thrombotic phenotypes than KO males. Notably, treatment of platelets from wild-type animals with globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) increased baseline platelet activation and aggregation. In contrast, several control GSLs did not stimulate platelet responses. These data suggest that chronically high concentrations of the Fabry-associated GSL, Gb3, contributes to the prothrombotic phenotypes experienced by Fabry patients by directly stimulating platelet activation.
Introduction

Fabry disease (MIM 301,500) is an inherited X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variations in the GLA gene (MIM 300,644, EC3.2.1.22) that decrease the activity of the lysosomal hydrolase alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-Gal A) and result in the accumulation of terminal galactose-containing substrates in the glycosphingolipid (GSL) metabolic pathway. Most prominently, the GSLs globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and its deacylated derivative globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) accumulate, but tissue deposition of these GSLs varies with the relative rates of sphingolipid metabolism in individual cell and tissue types and with the level of residual alpha-Gal A activity.

Recent epidemiological studies based on genetic screening suggest Fabry disease is the most prevalent of lysosomal storage disorders, and significantly more common than previously appreciated. For example, of approximately 200,000 newborns screened in Illinois Fabry disease occurred most frequently (1 in 8454 infants). In additional studies, GLA mutations associated with a classical presentation of the disease were present in approximately 1 in 50,000 males. In comparison, mutations associated with an atypical presentation or later-onset disease were present in approximately 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 8,000 males and 1 in 6,000 to 1 in 40,000 females. As newborn screening techniques continue to identify novel mutations in GLA that attenuate alpha-Gal A activity, the estimated prevalence of Fabry disease will likely continue to increase.

Classically, manifestations of Fabry disease begin in childhood with the appearance of corneal opacities, sweating abnormalities, and neuropathic or limb pain. During adolescence, dermatologic abnormalities (e.g., telangiectasias and angiokeratomas) and gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., diarrhea or constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting) often begin, while kidney dysfunction and hearing loss frequently develop during the succeeding decades. Notably, cardiovascular (e.g., hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrhythmias, valvular disease) and cerebrovascular complications (e.g., transient ischemic attacks, ischemic strokes) occur at a high rate among Fabry patients and account for the majority of deaths in patients of both genders.

While enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is a standard treatment, some patients may not respond due to the development of neutralizing antibodies or the inability of replacement  -Gal A to be trafficked to all affected tissues. Apart from ERT, chaperone-based therapy is available for a subset of Fabry patients with amenable GAL missense mutations [e.g., mutations that display a >= 1.2-fold increase in activity over baseline when treated with a pharmacological chaperone in a GLP-validated amenability assay]. For amenable mutations, chaperone treatment can reduce  -Gal A misfolding and improve  -Gal A lysosomal targeting and activity. However, even with ERT or chaperone-based therapies, the manifestations of Fabry disease still significantly reduce the quality of life and lifespan for both male and female patients, with most patients still requiring symptomatic treatment.

alpha-Gal A substrates accumulate in the vascular endothelium, vascular smooth muscle, and patient plasma, suggesting that several candidate pathways may contribute to an increased thrombotic risk. Recently, we developed a murine model of Fabry disease that closely recapitulates most human phenotypes, including ocular, cardiovascular, and neuropathic manifestations and the accumulation of GSLs in the plasma. Using this Fabry rat model lacking detectable  -Gal A enzyme activity, we investigated the possible mechanisms contributing to prothrombotic phenotypes in Fabry patients. In a recent study, we describe data demonstrating that knockout (KO) male rats accumulate  -Gal A substrates in their platelets and plasma and show a proinflammatory cytokine profile compared to normal animals. In addition, KO males had significant increases in several circulating white blood cell types, and their platelets were more responsive to activation by the platelet agonist ADP.

The current report expands on our previous study to examine how sex differences impact the pathology of Fabry disease by including  -Gal A-KO female and heterozygous female animals. Additionally, these studies investigate the direct effect of GSLs on the activation state of resting platelets and agonist responsiveness. To achieve this, platelets from male and female animals with normal  -Gal A activity were treated with Fabry-associated GSLs before assessing platelet activation markers at resting state or after agonist treatment. Overall, the combination of mass spectrometry, functional platelet assays, and histological studies performed here suggest that the GSL globotriaosylceramide significantly contributes to prothrombotic platelet phenotypes in Fabry disease.
Results
Animals lacking alpha-Gal A activity accumulate terminal galactose-containing GSLs and have increased CD3-positive T lymphocytes and CD68-positive monocytic cells in the bone marrow

The bone marrow is a crucial regulator of hematopoietic cell generation and development, and glycans and glycosphingolipids within the marrow help regulate differentiation. Additionally, changes in glycosphingolipid content in the marrow have been correlated with several types of cancers. In a previous study, we discovered that alpha-Gal A KO male rats had significant changes in the bone marrow environment. Males deficient in alpha-Gal A accumulated substantial amounts of terminal-galactose-containing molecules compared to wild-type males in the bone marrow, as assessed using Griffonia simplicifolia isolectin B4 (IB4), a lectin with high affinity for terminal alpha-galactose moieties, and consistent with the accumulation of terminal alpha-galactose-containing GSLs (e.g., Gb3 and lyso-Gb3) in the bone marrow environment. The accumulation of alpha-galactose-containing molecules in the bone marrow of KO males also correlated with significant increases in T lymphocytes and myeloid-derived monocytic cells in the bone marrow, as assessed using CD3 and CD68 specific antibodies.

Glycosphingolipids accumulate in the bone marrow of alpha-Gal A-deficient rats. Representative decalcified femur sections from (n = 6) WT, (n = 6) HET, or (n = 6) KO female rats at 52-weeks-old were incubated with (A) biotinylated Griffonia simplicifolia isolectin B4 (IB4), a lectin with a high affinity for terminal alpha-galactose before quantification in (B). (C) Femur sections were incubated with an anti-CD3 antibody that recognizes cells of T lymphocyte lineage before visualization and quantification in (D). (E) Femur sections were incubated with an anti-CD68 antibody that recognizes cells of monocytic or macrophage lineages before quantification in (F). Visualization was carried out using Streptavidin-HRP and 3,3'diaminobenzidine detection. Analysis of histological staining was performed by analyzing three random fields of view at 20X magnification using ImageJ. Data are reported as the mean +- SEM and compared using an ordinary One-Way ANOVA test with Tukey's multiple comparisons. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), **P < 0.005, ****P < 0.0001.

As Fabry disease is an X-linked disorder, the present study aimed to evaluate the accumulation of terminal alpha-galactose-containing molecules in the bone marrow of alpha-Gal A wild-type, heterozygous, and homozygous-KO females to define sex differences involved in the pathology of Fabry disease. Our results reveal that both heterozygote and homozygous-KO females exhibit significant increases in total areas of IB4 and CD3-staining, suggestive of an accumulation of alpha-galactose-containing GSLs (Figs. 1A-B) and an increase in the number of T lymphocytes in the bone marrow compared to wild-type females (Figs. 1C-D). However, relative to wild-type females, only alpha-Gal A-KO females display increased CD68-staining in the bone marrow, indicative of an increase in monocytic cells, whereas alpha-Gal A heterozygous females did not (Figs. 1E-F). In contrast, no differences are seen with CD41 staining, indicating the number of megakaryocytes within the bone marrow is similar among wild-type, heterozygous, and KO females (Fig. S1).

The accumulation of alpha-Gal A substrates in the circulation of alpha-Gal A-KO rats correlates with increases in circulating white blood cells and sera concentration of the proinflammatory cytokine tissue necrosis factor

Markers of chronic inflammation are elevated in alpha-Gal A-deficient rats. (A) Whole blood was drawn from the tail of WT, HET, and KO female rats (15- to 75-weeks old) and specific cell populations were counted using a Sysmex XP-300 hematological analyzer (Sysmex). Data are binned into 15-25, 25-50, and 50-75-week-old age groups from (n = 13-26) WT, (n = 14-23) HET, and (n = 18-25) KO female rats for each age group. Data are means +- SEM and compared using a Mixed-effects model with the Geisser-Greenhouse correction and Tukey's multiple comparisons test. Cytokine levels were measured from the plasma of (n = 12) WT and (n = 12) KO male rats (52 -75-weeks-old) (B) or from (n = 12) WT, (n = 12) HET, and (n = 12) KO female rats (C) using a multiplex flow cytometry assay. Data from males are means +- SEM and compared using multiple t-tests. Data from females are means +- SEM and compared using an ordinary One-Way ANOVA test with Tukey's multiple comparisons. P values are listed for TNF in panel C. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, ****P < 0.0001.

Due to the increased abundance of T lymphocytes and myeloid-derived monocytic cells observed in the bone marrow of alpha-Gal A-KO female rats and the increased abundance of circulating white blood cells previously observed in our characterization of alpha-Gal A-KO males, we assessed alpha-Gal A normal, heterozygote, and enzyme-KO females for changes in circulating blood counts (Fig. 2A and Fig. S2).

Like the bone marrow environment, alpha-Gal A-KO female animals had elevated levels of several circulating white blood cell types, including lymphocytes and monocytes, relative to age-matched animals with normal alpha-Gal A activity (Fig. 2A). Lymphocyte and monocyte counts increased in an age-dependent manner, with lymphocyte counts peaking between 25-50 weeks, and monocyte counts peaking between 50-75 weeks. In contrast, alpha-Gal A heterozygote females did not have increases in the number of circulating white blood cells (Fig. 2A).

Fabry patients have an increase in the concentration of the proinflammatory cytokines tissue necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Correspondingly, we found that alpha-Gal A-KO males had increases in circulating TNF, IL-13, IL-17A, and IL-22. To ascertain whether sex differences impact the cytokine profiles of male and female alpha-Gal A-deficient rats, we simultaneously quantified the abundance of several proinflammatory cytokines in male and female animals (Fig. 2B-C, Fig. S3, S4). Overall, we confirm that KO males had significantly higher concentrations of TNF in their circulation than males with normal alpha-Gal A activity (Fig. 2B). alpha-Gal A KO females also display an increase in circulating TNF levels, however this increase did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 2C; p = 0.0655). In contrast, IL-6 concentrations were not elevated in female or male alpha-Gal A-KO rats.

Sera from alpha-Gal A knockout animals of both sexes accumulate higher concentrations of alpha-Gal A substrates relative to wild-type animals, but knockout males accumulate several alpha-Gal A substrate GSLs to a greater extent than enzyme-deficient females

Terminal alpha-galactose containing glycosphingolipids accumulate in the serum of alpha-Gal A-deficient rats. (A) Glycosphingolipids were extracted from the serum of (n = 3) WT, (n = 3) HET, (n = 3) KO females (52-week-old), and (n = 3) WT and (n = 3) KO male (52-week-old) and analyzed using nanospray ionization-mass spectrometry (NSI-MS). Representative mass spectrometry spectra encompassing m/z ratios of 890-2000 are displayed for WT male, HET female, KO male, and KO female rats. (B) Glycosphingolipids isolated from the serum of WT, HET, and KO females or WT and KO males (C) were quantified relative to a known tetrasaccharide standard (DP4, red). Highlighted in pink are the  -galactosidase A substrates Gb3, globotriaosylceramide; lyso-Gb3, globotriaosylsphingosine; Gb3 + hexoside extension; lyso-Gb3 + hexoside extension; and B-group antigen. Data are means +- SEM. Data derived from female sera are compared using an ordinary One-Way ANOVA test with Tukey's multiple comparisons. Data derived from male sera are compared using multiple t-tests. P-values are listed above each comparison. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005.

To evaluate the extent that increases in the number of circulating white blood cells and proinflammatory cytokines correlate with the abundance of terminal alpha-galactose-containing GSLs in the circulation, GSLs were isolated from the sera of alpha-Gal A homozygous, heterozygous, and KO females and wild-type and hemizygous KO males. Isolated GSLs were then quantified by mass spectrometry (Fig. 3A). Increases in the abundance of several terminal alpha-galactose-containing GSLs (e.g., Gb3, lyso-Gb3, and B-group antigen) were observed in alpha-Gal A-KO females but not heterozygous animals. (Fig. 3B). KO males also show significant increases in alpha-Gal A substrate GSLs relative to normal males (Fig. 3C). Notably, males without alpha-Gal A activity accumulate significantly more of several Fabry-related GSL than KO females in their sera (e.g., Mean concentrations (pmol/mg) KO males versus KO Females; Gb3, 479.74 vs. 219.17; lyso-Gb3, 143.84 vs. 57.07; Blood Group B, 219.86 versus 33.39) (Fig. S5).
Prothrombotic platelet phenotypes correlate with the relative concentrations of alpha-Gal A substrate accumulation in platelets

Male, but not female, alpha-Gal A-deficient rats demonstrate prothrombotic platelet phenotypes. (A) Light transmission aggregomertry: platelet-rich plasma (PRP) was isolated from the whole blood of (n = 9) WT male, (n = 10) KO male, (n = 10) WT female, and (n = 9) KO female rats (50 to 65-week-old). PRP was diluted, and light transmission was continuously monitored for 500 s following the addition of ADP (30 muM). Data are presented as means +- SEM and were compared using an Unpaired t-test. P-values are listed above each comparison. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), **P < 0.005. (B) Functional platelet assays: washed platelets were isolated from the whole blood of WT, HET, and KO female rats (25-75-week-old) and binned into 25-50, or 50-75-week-old age groups. Flow cytometry assays were performed to measure fibrinogen binding following platelet treatment with ADP (30 muM) or convulxin (0.5 mg/mL) from (n = 14-21) WT, (n = 14-19) HET, and (n = 13-18) KO female rats. Data are presented as means +- SEM and compared using a Mixed-effects model and Tukey's multiple comparisons test. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05) (C) Microfluidics adhesion assays: whole blood from 50 to 65-week-old female rats was incubated with 50 muM mepacrine to fluorescently label platelets before being flowed (25 mL/h) over individual microfluidic channels coated with fibrinogen (50 mug/mL). Adherent platelets were imaged using an inverted microscope (EVOS cell imaging system). Three independent fields of view were analyzed for each rat (n = 10 WT, n = 8 HET, and n = 9 KO). Data are presented as means +- SEM and were compared using an Ordinary one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05).

In our previous study of male animals, platelets from alpha-Gal A-KO males were found to be hyper-responsive to agonist-mediated activation of PY-family receptors stimulated by ADP but not by agonist-mediated stimulation of PAR or GPVI receptors by thrombin or convulxin. In the current study, we directly compared male and female alpha-Gal A-deficient animals for differences in agonist-stimulated platelet activation using light transmission aggregometry (Fig. 4A). Female animals were also assessed for thrombotic platelet phenotypes using flow cytometry-based functional (Fig. 4B) and microfluidic platelet adhesion (Fig. 4C) assays. Although alpha-Gal A-KO male rats exhibit increased aggregation in response to ADP, neither heterozygous nor KO females show increased aggregation after ADP stimulation (Fig. 4A and S6). Similarly, heterozygote and KO females did not demonstrate a significant difference from wild-type females in a flow-cytometry-based functional assay (Fig. 4B) or a microfluidic-based fibrinogen adhesion assay (Fig. 4C) when platelets were stimulated by ADP or convulxin. No differences in P-selectin expression levels or annexin V binding were detected between younger and older wild-type, heterozygous or KO females (Fig. S7).

Terminal alpha-galactose containing glycosphingolipid accumulation in HET and KO platelets. (A) Glycosphingolipids were extracted from the platelets of (n = 3) WT, (n = 3) HET, (n = 3) KO females (52-week-old), and (n = 3) WT and (n = 3) KO male (52-week-old) and analyzed using nanospray ionization-mass spectrometry (NSI-MS). Representative mass spectrometry spectra encompassing intensity of peaks up to seven minutes are displayed for control, HET, and KO rats to highlight Gb3 accumulation. (B) Glycosphingolipids isolated from WT, HET, and KO females were quantified relative to a known tetrasaccharide standard (DP4). Highlighted in pink are the  -galactosidase A substrates Gb3, globotriaosylceramide; lyso-Gb3, globotriaosylsphingosine; Gb3 + hexoside extension; Gb3 + 2-hexoside extension, lyso-Gb3 + hexoside extension; lyso-Gb3 + 2-hexoside extension. The glycosphingolipids Gb4, globotriaosylceramide; GM3 ganglioside; and Lac, lactosylceramide were also quantified. Data are means +- SEM and were compared using an ordinary One-Way ANOVA test with Tukey's multiple comparisons. (C) Glycosphingolipids isolated from WT and KO males were quantified relative to a known tetrasaccharide standard (DP4). Highlighted in pink are the  -galactosidase A substrates Gb3, globotriaosylceramide; lyso-Gb3, globotriaosylsphingosine; Gb3 + hexoside extension; Gb3 + 2-hexoside extension, lyso-Gb3 + hexoside extension; lyso-Gb3 + 2-hexoside extension. The glycosphingolipids Gb4, globotriaosylceramide; GM3 ganglioside; and Lac, lactosylceramide were also quantified. Data are means +- SEM and were compared using multiple t-tests. P-values are listed above each comparison. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005.

passages.text: Due to the sex differences observed when comparing alpha-Gal A-KO male and female responses in platelet-based functional assays, platelet GSL content from alpha-Gal A-deficient animals of both sexes was quantified by mass spectrometry to determine whether the accumulation of alpha-Gal A terminal-galactose-containing substrates correlated with the sex differences observed in platelet-based functional assays (Fig. 5A). alpha-Gal A-KO male and female animals accumulate significantly more of the terminal-galactose-containing GSLs Gb3, and lyso-Gb3 than age and sex-matched wild-type animals (Figs. 5B-C). Strikingly, however, the accumulation of the alpha-Gal A substrate Gb3 was nearly two-fold higher in alpha-Gal A-KO males (mean; 391.19 fmol) than females (mean; 203.81 fmol). In comparison, lyso-Gb3 accumulated to a similar extent in alpha-Gal A-KO deficient male (mean; 233.56 fmol) and female (mean; 199.08 fmol) animals (Fig. S5). Interestingly, platelets from alpha-Gal A heterozygote females did not accumulate significantly higher levels of terminal-galactose-containing GSLs than wild-type females with normal alpha-Gal A activity (Figs. 5B-C). These findings suggest that phenotypic differences observed in alpha-Gal A-deficient male and female animals are caused by the accumulation of Gb3 above a threshold level achieved only by alpha-Gal A-KO males, but not alpha-Gal A-KO female animals.
Globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) alters platelets in a prothrombotic manner by increasing baseline platelet activation and sensitizing platelets to agonist-mediated activation

Globotriaosylceramide alters platelets in a prothrombotic manner. (A) Washed platelets were isolated from the whole blood of WT male and female rats (50-65-week-old) and incubated +- glycosphingolipids or DMSO vehicle for 1 h at 25  C. Flow cytometry assays were used to measure fibrinogen binding to the platelet glycoprotein complex GPIIbeta/IIIalpha following platelet activation +- ADP (30 muM) using a BD-LSRII flow cytometer. (B) Washed platelets from WT male and female rats were incubated with a combination of acylated and deacylated glycosphingolipids: 10 muM Gb3/2 muM Lyso-Gb3 (blue), 1 muM Gb3/ 0.2 muM Lyso-Gb3 (red), 10 muM GC/ 2 muM Lyso-GC (purple), and 1 muM GC/ 0.2 muM Lyso-GC (orange) or DMSO vehicle (green) and fibrinogen binding was measured following platelet activation +- ADP from (n = 15) WT males and (n = 14) WT females. Data are means +- SEM and were compared using a Mixed-effects model and Dunnett's multiple comparisons test. (C) Washed platelets from WT male and female rats were incubated with individual acylated or deacylated glycosphingolipids; 10 muM Gb3 (blue), 2 muM Lyso-Gb3 (red), 10 muM GC (purple), and 2 muM Lyso-GC (orange) or DMSO vehicle (green) and fibrinogen binding was measured following platelet activation +- ADP from (n = 16) WT males and (n = 17) WT females. Data are means +- SEM and compared using a Mixed-effects model and Dunnett's multiple comparisons test. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), *P < 0.05, **P < 0.005, ***P < 0.0005, and ****P < 0.0001.

Globotriaosylceramide alters platelets in a prothrombotic manner. (A) Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) was isolated from the whole blood of WT male and female rats. Light transmission was continuously measured for 600 s following +- glycosphingolipids (GSL) treatment to the PRP cuvette at 37  C. After 600 s, ADP (30 muM) or vehicle control was added to the PRP, and light transmission was recorded for an additional 300 s. PRP was isolated from the whole blood of (B) (n = 7-12) WT and (n = 8-9) KO male rats (50 to 65-week-old) or (C) from the whole blood of (n = 7-12) WT female, and (n = 8-9) KO female rats (50 to 65-week-old)and aggregation was measured for the following conditions: WT with no ADP (grey), KO with no ADP (pink), WT with ADP (black), KO with ADP (red), WT with 10 muM Gb3 (blue), WT with 10 muM Gb3 and ADP (purple), WT with 10 muM GC (green), and WT with 10 muM GC and ADP (orange). Data are means +- SEM and compared using unpaired t - tests. ns, not significant (P >= 0.05), ***P < 0.005, ****P < 0.0001.

To determine whether the Fabry disease-associated GSL Gb3 was capable of directly eliciting thrombotic platelet phenotypes, platelets isolated from male and female animals with normal alpha-Gal A activity were treated with pairs of acylated and deacylated GSLs that either included Gb3 (e.g., Gb3 + lyso-Gb3) or did not include Gb3 [e.g., glucosylceramide (GlcCer) and glucosylsphingosine (lyso-GlcCer)]. GlcCer was utilized as a control due to its similar ceramide-based structure. However, whereas GlcCer terminates with a single glucose molecule, Gb3 contains a trisaccharide that terminates with galactose (Fig. S8). GSL-treated platelets were then assessed for platelet activation in a flow cytometry-based functional platelet assay (Fig. 6A). Strikingly, the combination of Gb3 and lyso-Gb3 elicited a dose-dependent activation of resting platelets as assessed by fibrinogen binding (10 microM Gb3/2 microM Lyso-Gb3, fold change in fibrinogen binding, males, 5.13-fold increase; Females, 5.18-fold increase), and sensitized platelets to ADP-mediated activation relative to platelets treated with the combination of GlcCer and lyso-GlcCer (Fig. 6B). Moreover, when platelet activation assays were performed using male and female platelets isolated from wild-type animals and then treated with individual GSLs, only the addition of Gb3 significantly increased baseline platelet activation (10 microM Gb3, fold change in fibrinogen binding, Males, 6.47-fold increase; Females; 6.81-fold increase) and responsiveness to ADP (Figs. 6C, and S9). Similar results were observed when platelets with normal alpha-Gal A activity were treated with Gb3, or control GSLs, in the presence or absence of ADP and assessed by light-transmission aggregometry (Fig. 7A). In these experiments, the addition of Gb3 to platelets isolated from male or females with normal alpha-Gal A activity significantly increased the aggregation of resting platelets relative to platelets treated with the control GSL glucosylceramide (Figs. 7B-C, Fig. S10).
Discussion

Our previous studies used a Fabry rat model to identify possible mechanisms contributing to prothrombotic phenotypes in Fabry patients. In these studies, male rats lacking the enzyme  -Gal A accumulated GSL substrates in their platelets, serum, and bone marrow. They also displayed a proinflammatory cytokine profile compared to animals with  -Gal A activity. In addition, KO males had significant increases in several circulating white blood cell types, and their platelets were more responsive to activation by the platelet agonist ADP..

Here, we expanded our previous studies in two directions. First, we characterized the extent to which  -Gal A heterozygote and  -Gal A-KO female rats experience prothrombotic phenotypes. Second, we define the extent to which Fabry disease-associated GSLs directly impact platelet biology to increase thrombotic risk.

In the first aspect of the study,  -Gal-A-deficient female and male animals demonstrated similar disease manifestations and indicators of chronic inflammation. The histological analysis of the bone marrow from 52-week-old females stained with Griffonia simplicifolia isolectin B4, a lectin with high specificity for terminal-galactose-containing GSLs, revealed striking accumulations of glycosphingolipids in the bone marrow of females with attenuated  -Gal A activity, similar to  -Gal A-KO males (Fig. 1A). Both male and female Fabry animals also had chronically high levels of white blood cells in their bone marrow (Figs. 1A-B) and circulation, and displayed significantly elevated lymphocyte and monocyte counts compared to age- and sex-matched cohorts with normal  -Gal A activity (Fig. 2A). Additionally, both male and female  -Gal A-KO animals had elevated tumor necrosis factor concentrations in plasma, suggestive of chronic inflammation (Fig. 2B). These data are consistent with clinical studies reporting elevated TNF concentrations in Fabry patients, and studies reporting the enhancement of a feedback loop whereby elevated levels of Gb3 lead to the increased expression of tumor necrosis factor, which, in turn, further stimulates sphingolipid production. Notably, TNF antagonists have been FDA-approved for treating several inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease, and could be assessed for their ability to dampen systemic inflammation and attenuate similar symptomologies experienced by Fabry patients..

In this study we also report that female  -Gal A-KO rats had drastically different GSL profiles in their sera and platelets compared to females with normal  -Gal A activity (Figs. 3 and 5). However, compared to male  -Gal A-KO rats, KO females, on average, accumulated less of several Fabry-associated GSLs in their sera and platelets than age-matched males (Figs. 3, 5, and Fig. S5). Correspondingly, platelets isolated from  -Gal A-deficient females were not sensitized to agonist-mediated activation or aggregation, unlike platelets isolated from hemizygous KO males (Fig. 4 and Fig. S6), suggesting that a threshold level of GSL accumulation must be met to elicit these thrombotic platelet phenotypes.

Although  -Gal A heterozygote and KO female animals accumulated lower concentrations of Fabry-associated GSLs than males in our study, the thrombotic phenotypes experienced by affected heterozygote female Fabry patients may strongly depend on factors that impact residual  -Gal A activity and the resultant accumulation of GSLs. For example, patterns of X-chromosome inactivation in various cell and tissue types in heterozygotic Fabry females may play a prominent role in determining the severity of clinical manifestations of the disease. Plasma concentration Gb3 ranges have been reported between approximately 3-11 microM in hemizygous males and between 1-4 microM in heterozygous female Fabry patients. Although, on average, Gb3 concentrations are lower among heterozygous females, a significant overlap exists among hemizygous male and heterozygous female cohorts in the 3-4 microM range. Additionally, plasma Gb3 concentrations in these studies did not significantly differ based on ERT treatment status. Thus, retrospectively examining the correlation between plasma Gb3 levels and the incidence of thrombotic events among subgroups of Fabry patients may help to evaluate further the strength of the relationship between plasma Gb3 concentrations and thrombotic risk.

To assess the ability of Gb3 and lyso-Gb3 to directly impact platelet biology, platelets were isolated from healthy animals with normal  -Gal A activity and then treated with GSLs at concentrations found among Fabry patients with classical disease presentation (10 microM Gb3 and 2 microM lyso-Gb3, or 10 microM Gb3 alone) or with control GSLs (10 microM glucocerebroside and 2 microM lyso-glucocerebroside) at the same concentrations. Strikingly, only the Fabry-associated GSL, Gb3, was sufficient to stimulate increased baseline platelet activation as assessed by fibrinogen binding (Fig. 6C) and platelet aggregation (Fig. 7B-C). Adding Gb3 alone also increased platelet responsiveness to ADP in functional platelet assays assessing fibrinogen binding (Fig. 6B). These data are remarkable in that they suggest that chronically high concentrations of the Fabry disease-associated GSL, Gb3, can directly stimulate platelet activation and increase platelet responsiveness to agonist-mediated activation.

Apart from the data presented here, gangliosides and glycosphingolipids have been shown to be capable of modifying cellular responses to extracellular signals. For example, the oligosaccharide portion of the ganglioside GM1, can transduce extracellular signals through the plasma membrane when the oligosaccharide portion of GM1 interacts with the transmembrane protein complex TrkA-NGF, whereas, the ganglioside GM3 has been demonstrated to inhibit human epidermal growth factor receptor. Notably, interactions between the GSL lactosylceramide and the tyrosine protein kinase Lyn have been shown to negatively regulate FcgammaRIIa receptors on the surface of immune cells. Finally, Gb3 itself has been shown in vitro, to interact with the glycosphingolipid binding motif of Fas, a TNF-receptor family member important for the induction of apoptosis. In this current study, the data suggest that the terminal and penultimate galactose residues of Gb3 are essential for eliciting prothrombotic platelet changes, as the closely related GSL glucosylceramide, which shares an identical ceramide-based structure with Gb3, but which terminates with a single glucose moiety, failed to elicit similar platelet changes.

Overall, these findings underscore the direct role of Gb3 in eliciting thrombotic platelet phenotypes, shedding a light on its potential contribution to the heightened risk of thrombosis observed in Fabry disease patients and providing further rationale to evaluate the effectiveness of platelet inhibitors in reducing thrombotic burden and the incidence of cerebrovascular and cardiovascular complications in female and male Fabry patients.

Our observations have led us to hypothesize several potential mechanisms by which Gb3 may impact platelet biology. One possibility is that Gb3 directly interacts with platelet receptors such as FcgammaRIIa or PY-family receptors, resulting in downstream signaling that favors platelet activation. Alternatively, as we have noted that Gb3 increases baseline platelet activation and sensitizes platelets to activation by ADP, another hypothesis is that Gb3 may alter the composition of platelet membranes, resulting in conformational changes in platelet membrane components that lead to activation signaling and increased sensitization to agonist-mediated activation. In future studies, it will be crucial to further define the mechanisms by which Gb3 affects platelet activation and to include evaluating the impact of Gb3 on platelets obtained from healthy human donors.
Methods
Animals

Male and female dark agouti (DA) rats were initially acquired from Taconic Biosciences, Inc. (Rensselaer, NY). The Fabry rat model (Dark Agouti background), completely deficient in alpha-galactosidase A activity, was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, as we described previously. The wild-type (WT), knockout (KO), and heterozygous female (HET) rats were obtained from the existing Fabry rat colony at the Medical College of Wisconsin. The rats were provided free access to chow (Purina, diet 5001) and drinking water and were maintained on a 12-h light/dark cycle. All animal procedures were carried out following the recommendations in The National Research Council Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Medical College of Wisconsin (Protocol Number: AUA00004621). For this study, male and female rats 15-75 weeks-of-age were used. Rats were euthanized by compressed CO2 and bilateral pneumothorax. All methods are reported in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines.
Femur isolation

Rats were euthanized, and hind-limb femurs were removed intact from the acetabulum and below the knee. Connective tissue and muscle were removed from dissected femurs, and the isolated femurs were utilized for histology and immunohistochemistry.
Histology and immunohistochemistry

Rat femurs were fixed in 10% (v/v) neutral buffered formalin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) for 24-72 h as previously described. Following fixation, femurs were treated with ethanol (Decon Laboratories, Prussia, PA, USA) for dehydration, cleared with xylene (Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Hesse, Germany), and infiltrated and embedded with paraffin (Sakura, Finetek, Tokyo, Honshu, Japan). Paraffin blocks were cut into 4 mum sections before being mounted on poly-L-lysine-coated slides (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Antigens were visualized using streptavidin-biotin detection. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating slides to 95  C, addition of BOND epitope retrieval solution two (AR9640; Leica, Buffalo Grove, Il, USA), and a 12-min cooldown. For lectin staining, slides were incubated with biotinylated Griffonia simplicifolia isolectin B4 (IB4, 5 mug/ml; Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA, USA), and then incubated with streptavidin-HRP and 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (Agilent, Madison, WI, USA) to detect alpha-galactosyl glycoconjugates. For antibody staining, slides were incubated with anti-CD68 (ED-1 clone, MAB1435, 1:100; MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA, USA), anti-CD3 (A0452, 1:200; Agilent, Madison, WI, USA), or anti-CD41 (ab181582, 1:500; Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA) antibodies and areas of staining were visualized by streptavidin-biotin detection using biotinylated secondary antibodies, streptavidin-HRP, and 3,3'diaminobenzidine detection. High-resolution images were obtained with a NanoZoomer 2.0-HT digital slide scanner (Hamamatsu Photonics, Hamamatsu, Honshu, Japan). For immunohistology quantification, three independent sections from each animal were analyzed at 20X magnification and quantified using Image J2 version 2.14.0/1.54f. Build: c89e8500e4; https://imagej.net/.
Whole blood isolation

Whole blood (900 muL) was drawn from the tail artery using a 25-gauge needle (BD, East Rutherford, NJ, USA) into sterile syringes containing 3.2% (w/v) sodium citrate (100 muL). The blood was inverted seven times and added to sterile microfuge tubes. Following the blood draws, whole blood or blood components were immediately used for downstream assays.
Complete blood counts

Whole blood was diluted 1:7 (v/v) in DCL buffer (Sysmex, Kobe, Hyogo, Japan). Following dilution, whole blood samples were counted by Sysmex XP-300 hematological analyzer to obtain blood count values.
Platelet isolation

Whole blood was centrifuged at 250 x g for 8 min at 25  C, and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) was transferred to a new tube. A second centrifugation was then performed at 1000 x g for 5 min at 25  C and platelets were resuspended in 500 muL of modified Tyrode's Solution (20 mM Hepes, 135 mM NaCl, 6 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 5.6 mM D-glucose, pH 7.40) Platelets were counted by a hematological analyzer as above, resuspended in Tyrode's buffer at a concentration of 300,000 platelets/muL, and immediately used in platelet assays. An additional centrifugation step and resuspension of platelets in an appropriate buffer was performed as above to obtain washed platelets for subsequent biochemical analyses or cell-based assays.
Cytokine quantification

Cytokines were quantified based on manufacturer recommendations using a LegendPlex assay for rat cytokines (Biolegend, San Diego, CA, USA). In brief, plasma for cytokine quantification was obtained by centrifugation of whole blood for 10 min at 1,000 x g at room temperature, and plasma was immediately used to quantify circulating cytokine levels. A 96-well V-bottom polypropylene plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was then blocked (LegendPlex assay kit, Biolegend). Sample wells were then aspirated to remove buffer, and 25 muL of assay buffer and 25 muL of plasma were added to individual sample wells. Following plasma addition, antibody-coated beads were vortexed for 30 s, and 25 muL of mixed beads were added to each sample well with gentle mixing. The plate was then sealed, wrapped with aluminum foil, and placed on a shaker to incubate for two hours at 25  C. Following primary incubation, the plate was centrifuged at 1,000 x g for 5 min at 25  C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was removed, and beads were resuspended in wash buffer and centrifuged again at 1,000 x g for 5 min at 25  C. After removing the wash buffer, 25 muL of detection antibodies were added to each sample well. The plate was then sealed, wrapped with aluminum foil, and placed on a shaker at 800 RPM for one hour at 25  C. Following incubation, 25 muL of SA-PE reagent was added to each well for fluorescent detection of cytokines, and the plate was placed on a shaker at 800 RPM for 30 min at 25  C. Using a multichannel pipet, 200 muL of wash buffer was added to each well, and the plate was centrifuged at 1,000 x g for 5 min at 25  C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was removed, beads were resuspended with 150 muL wash buffer, and flow cytometry was performed using an Accuri C6 flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lake, NJ, USA).
Platelet activation assay

A 96-well V-bottom polypropylene plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was blocked with 1% BSA (w/v) in modified Tyrode's Solution, and 3 x 105 platelets in modified Tyrode's Solution with 1% BSA were added to each assay well. Activation assays were adapted from the work of Nylander and Lindahl. Platelets were incubated with AF488 fluorescently labeled fibrinogen (Thermo Fisher Scientific, F12191) for 30 min and activated with agonist for 15 min using 30 muM ADP (Sigma-Aldrich, A2754), 5 mg/mL convulxin (Santa Cruz), or 1% BSA in modified Tyrode's Solution as a negative control. Following platelet activation, fibrinogen binding was analyzed using an LSRII flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).
Platelet activation with glycosphingolipids

Following centrifugation steps during platelet isolation, platelets were resuspended in modified Tyrode's Solution. A 96-well V-bottom polypropylene plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was blocked using modified Tyrode's Solution. Platelets were incubated with AF488 fluorescently labeled fibrinogen (Thermo Fisher Scientific, F12191) and specified glycosphingolipid (GSL) concentration or DMSO (Thermo Fischer Scientific) vehicle for one hour at 25  C. Following the initial incubation, 3 x 105 platelets in modified Tyrode's Solution were added to each assay well, and platelets were activated with agonist for 15 min using 30 muM ADP (Sigma - Aldrich, A2754) or modified Tyrode's Solution. Following platelet activation, platelets were analyzed with an LSRII flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).
Platelet aggregation assay

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) was isolated from whole blood by centrifugation at 250 x g for eight minutes at 25  C and removing the top layer post-centrifugation. Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) was obtained from whole blood by performing a second centrifugation of PRP at 10,000 x g for 15 min at 4  C to remove residual cells. PPP was used as a negative control in aggregometry studies and to baseline the aggregometer. For PRP, platelet concentration was determined using a hematological analyzer and adjusted to 300 x 103 platelets/muL with modified Tyrode's Solution. A total of 300 muL of PRP or PPP as a negative control, was added to glass cuvettes and placed in a Chrono-log Model 700 Whole-blood/Optical Lumi-aggregometer (Chrono-log, Havertown, PA, USA). Light transmittance was recorded for 30 s before platelet-rich plasma, and PPP channels of the aggregometer were simultaneously zeroed to baseline using the PPP. ADP (30 muM) (Sigma - Aldrich, A2754) was then added to each cuvette, and light transmission was recorded for a minimum of five minutes at 37  C.
Platelet aggregation assay with the addition of glycosphingolipids

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and platelet-poor plasma (PPP) were obtained as detailed above and adjusted to 300 x 103 platelets/muL with modified Tyrode's Solution. A total of 300uL of PRP or PPP + DMSO (Thermo Fischer Scientific) vehicle was added to glass cuvettes and placed in a Chrono-log Model 700 Whole-blood/Optical Lumi-aggregometer (Chrono-log, Havertown, PA, USA). Light transmittance was recorded for 30 s before platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and PPP channels of the aggregometer were simultaneously zeroed to baseline using the PPP. 10 muM of designated glycosphingolipid (GSL) was then added to the PRP cuvette, and light transmission was recorded for a minimum of 10 min at 37  C. After 10 min, 30 muM ADP (Sigma - Aldrich, A2754) was added to each cuvette, and light transmission was recorded for an additional 5 min at 37  C.
Generation of stock solutions of commercially obtained glycosphingolipids

Glycosphingolipids (GSLs), ceramide trihexoside (Gb3), lyso-ceramide trihexoside (lyso-Gb3), glucocerebrosides, buttermilk (GC), and glucosylsphingosine, buttermilk (lyso-GC) were all obtained from Matreya (Matreya, catalog No: 1067, 1520, 1521, and 1306). Each lyophilized GSL was resuspended in DMSO (Thermo Fischer Scientific) as a 1.0 mg/mL stock solution and stored at -20  C. For experimental use, stock solutions of GSLs were further diluted using DMSO (Thermo Fischer Scientific) as needed.
Assessment of platelet adhesion under flow conditions

A microfluidic adhesion assay was adapted from Manz et al., and we have previously detailed this assay. In brief, fibrinogen (341,576; MilleporeSigma) was immobilized by adding 20 muL of fibrinogen diluted in Hepes buffer to a final concentration of 50 mug/mL in each microfluidic channel of an Ibidi mu-slide VI 0.4 chip (80,601; Ibidi, Fitchburg, WI, USA). Microfluidic chips were then incubated overnight at 4  C inside of a 100 mm petri dish wrapped in parafilm to prevent evaporation. Following fibrinogen immobilization, each microfluidic channel was blocked for two hours at room temperature with 200 muL of 1% BSA in Hepes buffer. Whole blood was then isolated as described above and, following isolation, was incubated with 50 muM Mepacrine (Q3251; MilliporeSigma) at 25  C for 15 min to fluorescently label platelet dense granules. To assemble the microfluidic flow system, two 16-inch sections of 0.8 mm I.D. silicone tubing (10,841, Ibidi) were connected to a straight female luer lock connector (10,825; Ibidi) on one side, and an elbow male luer lock connector (10,802, Ibidi) on the opposite side. To prevent clotting, 1% BSA in Hepes buffer was drawn through the silicone tubing and into a 20 mL BD syringe (309,661; BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). The silicone tubing was then connected to the microfluidic slide using the elbow luer connectors, and the syringe was inserted into a syringe pump apparatus (New Era Pump 4000; New Era Pump Systems, Farmingdale, NY, USA). For microfluidic assays, the syringe pump was adjusted to a 25 mL/hr flow rate, and the syringe diameter setting was adjusted to 19.05 mm. Whole blood was then diluted 1:1 with 1% BSA in Hepes buffer and recalcified with 10 muM CaCl2/MgCl2. Following dilution and recalcification, whole blood was activated with 30 muM ADP, and flow through the microfluidic chamber was started immediately following platelet activation. For imaging of platelet adherence on immobilized fibrinogen, one image was collected every 10 s using an EVOS inverted microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 20X magnification for five minutes. The number of adherent platelets was then analyzed at 20X magnification and quantified using Image J software.
Quantification of lyso-glycosphingolipids

We have previously developed a method to quantitatively profile lyso-type glycosphingolipids following N-acetylation of the free amine group of sphingosine. Briefly, purified glycosphingolipids were N-acetylated, dried, and then subjected to permethylation. The N-acetylated and O-permethylated glycosphingolipids containing lyso-glycosphingolipids were then infused for nanospray ionization mass spectrometry (NSI-MS) with reference to the standard for quantitative analysis. This approach was used to compare glycosphingolipids and lyso-GSLs isolated from plasma or platelets. To detect lyso-glycosphingolipids species in the rat samples, TIM profiles were filtered for neutral loss of C18-sphingosine (Delta mass = 351, singly charged) to evaluate the concentration of lyso-GSL species.
Mass spectrometry

According to the previously described method of Anumula and Taylor, 1-3 microg of tC18-purified GSLs were permethylated with 12C-methyliodide before MS analysis. Maltotetraose oligosaccharide (Dp4) was permethylated with 13C-methyliodide and spiked into permethylated GSLs as a reference standard for GSL quantification. Permethylated GSLs were reconstituted in methanol/2-propanol/1-propanol/water (16:3:3:2 by volume) containing 1 mM NaOH for direct infusion into the mass spectrometer. Ten picomoles of 13C-permethylated Dp4 standard was added into the reconstituted permethylated GSL samples, and the mixture was analyzed by direct infusion into an ion trap mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Velos; Thermo Fisher Scientific) using a nanoelectrospray source, syringe flow rate of 0.6 mL/min and temperature set to 210 C. The instrument was tuned in positive ion mode using permethylated GSLs and Dp4 standards. For fragmentation by collision-induced dissociation (CID) in MS/MS and MSn, a normalized collision energy of 35% was used. Detection and absolute quantification of GSLs were accomplished using total ion mapping (TIM) and neutral loss scan (NL scan) functionalities of the Xcalibur software package version 2.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), as previously described. For TIM, the m/z range from 600 to 2000 was scanned in 2.4 mass unit windows with an overlap of 0.4 mass units. GSLs were identified as singly, doubly, and triply charged, sodiated species [M + Na] in positive mode, and peak intensities for all charge states were deconvoluted and summed for quantification. The major MS/MS fragment ions produced by CID of GSL preparations correspond to neutral loss of the ceramide moiety, leaving an intact GSL oligosaccharide ion for subsequent fragmentation in MSn. Therefore, an NL scan workflow was designed to acquire MSn fragmentation when an MS/MS profile contained a fragment ion with an m/z equivalent to losing the most prevalent ceramide moiety. After the data-dependent acquisition, the workflow returned to the full MS, excluding the parent ion, which was just fragmented, and chose the peak of the next highest intensity for MS/MS and MSn analysis. Using this data-dependent acquisition workflow, GSL glycan profiles and MSn sequencing were rapidly acquired for complex mixtures of GSLs. Permethylated GSLs were analyzed from multiple biological replicates from plasma (n = 3 for WT male and female, n = 3 for KO male and female, and n = 3 homozygous female) along with platelets (n = 3 for WT male and female, n = 3 for KO male and female, and n = 3 homozygous female). For all samples, GSLs were characterized by MS. The MS-based glycomics data generated in these analyses and the associated annotations are presented in accordance with the MIRAGE standards, the Athens Guidelines, and the broadly accepted SNFG symbol nomenclature for glycans. The MS raw data is deposited into the publicly available data repository tool, GlycoPost; the accession number is (GPST000428).

passages.text: Targeted intracellular delivery of molecular cargo to hypoxic human breast cancer stem cells
Abstract

Cancer stem cells (CSCs) drive tumorigenesis, are responsible for metastasis, and resist conventional therapies thus posing significant treatment challenges. CSCs reside in hypoxic tumor regions and therefore, effective therapies must target CSCs within this specific microenvironment. CSCs are characterized by limited distinguishable features, however, surface displayed phosphatidylserine (PS) appears to be characteristic of stem cells and offers a potential target. GlaS, a truncated coagulation protein that is internalized after binding PS, was investigated for intracellular delivery of molecular payloads to CSCs. Intracellular delivery via GlaS was enhanced in patient-derived CD44+ mammary CSCs under hypoxic conditions relative to physoxia or hyperoxia. In vivo , GlaS successfully targeted hypoxic tumor regions, and functional delivery of molecular cargo was confirmed using luciferin conjugated to GlaS via a disulfide linkage (GlaS-SS-luc), which releases luciferin upon intracellular glutathione reduction. Bioluminescence imaging demonstrated effective GlaS-mediated delivery of luciferin, a model drug, to CSCs in culture and in vivo . These findings offer the promise of directed delivery of therapeutic agents to intracellular targets in CSCs.
