passages.text: Oxidative stress injury

Stone formation is closely associated with an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) within the kidney. ROS generated during aerobic metabolism encompass diverse molecules such as superoxide anion, nitric oxide free radical, hydroxyl, hydrogen peroxide, and so on. In general, the production and clearance of cellular ROS are balanced to maintain physiological functions. However, under certain pathological circumstances, such as stimulation by calcium oxalate (CaOx) crystals or elevated concentrations of oxalate or calcium, the production of ROS escalates while clearance mechanisms become insufficient. This imbalance leads to oxidative stress injury and then promotes the adhesion of crystals to renal tubular epithelial cells.

SIRT1 is an NAD-dependent protein deacetylase showing anti-inflammatory and antioxidative functions. found that miR-128-3p was upregulated in the kidneys of CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice and it suppressed the expression of SIRT1 by binding its 3'-UTR. Theaflavin supplementation could alleviate CaOx-induced renal oxidative stress injury by inhibiting miR-128-3p while upregulating SIRT1. In our previous study, we demonstrated that the expression of miR-155-5p was increased in HK-2 cells cocultured with COM and that miR-155-5p could directly target matrix Gla protein (MGP). Additionally, miR-155-5p antagonist significantly reduced renal crystal disposition and ROS generation in CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats. reported that the expression of miR-30c-5p expression was significantly downregulated in HK-2 cells treated with sodium oxalate. Overexpression of miR-30c-5p reversed apoptosis, crystal deposition, lactate dehydrogenase, malondialdehyde and ROS levels in the kidneys of CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice by targeting autophagy protein 5 (ATG5). In addition, another study has shown that supplementation with miR-204 agonists could reduce CaOx-induced oxidative stress injury in renal tubular epithelial cells, offering potential targets for preventing stone formation.

It has been reported that NACHT, LRR and PYD domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) plays a crucial role in inflammation. Lv et al. found that miR-223-3p bound to the 3'-UTR of both NLRP3 and lncRNA X inactive specific transcript (XIST). CaOx could upregulate the expression of XIST, which competitively bound to miR-223-3p, leading to the release of NLRP3 mRNA from miR-223-3p in renal tubular epithelial cells. These competing interactions between XIST/miRNA-223/NLRP3 ultimately exacerbated the production of ROS, inflammatory injury, and crystal deposition in the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice. Similarly, studies regarding XIST sponging miRNAs to activate NLRP3 inflammasome in other diseases have also been reported. Evidence has shown that lncRNA H19 is involved in inflammatory regulation and induces tissue injury. Genome-wide expression profile analysis of renal tissue with Randall's plaques demonstrated that H19 expression was upregulated. found that miR-216b bound to the 3'-UTR of both H19 and high mobility group protein B1 (HMGB1). H19 could activate the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-kappaB pathway by competitively binding miR-216b in the kidney. This activation subsequently induced oxidative stress injury and promoted stone formation. reported that the expression of lncRNA ATB was increased, while the expression of miR-200a was decreased in HK-2 cells after incubation with COM. Further investigation revealed that miR-200a directly bound to the 3'-UTR of lncRNA ATB, as confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter experiment. ATB promoted ROS generation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and apoptosis to contribute to CaOx-induced renal injury by sponging miR-200a. It should be indicated that competing regulations between ATB and miR-200 family also played a role in the pathogenesis of carcinoma and neurotoxicity. found that the expression of miR-484 was downregulated in the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats. MiR-484 could upregulate the expression of forkhead box protein O1 (FoxO1) by targeting Vitamin D receptor (VDR), then suppressing apoptosis and oxidative stress injury in renal tubular epithelial cells. reported that miR-184 was upregulated in both the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats and renal tubular epithelial cells (HK-2) cultured with COM. This miRNA is capable of directly binding to the 3'-UTR of insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R), subsequently promoting COM-induced oxidative stress injury and apoptosis in renal tubular epithelial cells.
Inflammation

In recent years, increasing attention has been given to the role of the immune response in kidney stone formation. The lithogenic microenvironment can continuously stimulate renal tubular epithelial cells to secrete inflammatory factors. This results in an amplified inflammatory response that leads to renal tissue damage, promoting adhesion, aggregation, and growth of urine crystals. Moreover, macrophages are significantly increased in the kidneys of patients with CaOx nephrolithiasis, indicating their involvement in the immune regulation. Studies have shown that M1 macrophages secrete proinflammatory factors and promote kidney stone formation, whereas M2 macrophages secrete anti-inflammatory factors and play a role in inhibiting stone formation.

reported that lncRNA HOXA11-AS was upregulated in the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice, while miR-124-3p was downregulated. It was observed that miR-124-3p had the ability to bind to the 3'-UTR of both monocyte chemotactic protein 1 (MCP-1) and HOXA11-AS. LncRNA HOXA11-AS acted as a competing endogenous RNA to promote apoptosis, aggravate cellular damage and upregulate MCP-1 expression by sponging miR-124-3p, thereby mediating CaOx crystal-related renal inflammation. Macrophage colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) can recruit macrophages and promote M2 polarization. found that androgen receptor upregulated miR-185-5p by binding to the androgen response element on its 5' promoter in renal tubular epithelial cells. Dual luciferase reporter experiments showed that miR-185-5p bound to the 3'-UTR of CSF-1. Silencing the androgen receptor (AR) in renal tubular epithelial cells lead to upregulation of CSF-1 expression by downregulating miR-185-5p. This ultimately promoted macrophage recruitment and M2 polarization, which reduced renal crystal disposition in CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats.

The interferon regulatory factor (IRF) family is a class of important nuclear transcription factors that regulate the polarization of macrophages. The expression of IRF-1 is increased in the kidneys of mice with hyperoxaluria, and IRF-1 is considered to play a lithogenic role. found that nuclear factor erythroid 2-related 2 (Nrf2) exhibited positive transcriptional activation of miR-93-5p by binding to its promoter. MiR-93-5p could target IRF1 and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) mRNAs to inhibit their expression in macrophages. Sulforaphane, a pharmacological activator of Nrf2, could promote M2 macrophage polarization to suppress renal inflammation and crystal adhesion in CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice. Pioglitazone has also been reported to negatively regulate IRF1 expression by upregulating miR-23 in macrophages and then decreasing CaOx nephrocalcinosis. In another study by, bioinformatics analysis and chromatin immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) in bone marrow-derived macrophages could bind the promoter to transcriptionally activate miR-142a-3p. This activation subsequently inhibited the expression of IRF1 and HIF-1alpha by directly targeting their 3'-UTRs. AhR activation could diminish M1 macrophage polarization and promote M2 polarization to suppress CaOx nephrocalcinosis via the miR-142a-IRF1/HIF-1alpha pathway. In addition, reported that adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs)-derived miR-23-enriched exosomes could inhibit the polarization of M1 macrophages and protects against CaOx stone formation by directly targeting IRF1 in macrophages. found that miR-493-3p bound to the 3'-UTR of the macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF). Acetate supplementation could enhance the H3K9 and H3K27 acetylation levels at the promoter region of miR-493-3p, subsequently upregulating miR-493-3p and downregulating MIF expression. This process decreased macrophage infiltration, therefore attenuating hyperoxaluria-induced renal injury.
Osteogenic transformation

Randall's plaque is an ectopic calcification located in the renal papillary interstitium. Its main component is hydroxyapatite, which is similar to the bone matrix. The plaque can gradually grow into the renal interstitium and eventually break through the urothelium and contact urine. Early-formed urinary crystals can adhere to the plaque and then form stones. Therefore, Randall's plaque is considered to be the origin of kidney stones by many researchers. It has been reported that osteogenic transformation of cells in the renal collecting system, including renal tubular epithelial cells and renal interstitial fibroblasts, plays a role in the formation of Randall's plaque.

identified a series of ncRNAs that regulated the osteogenic transformation of renal interstitial fibroblasts in a lithogenic microenvironment. They found that the expression of miR-410-3p was decreased in renal interstitial fibroblasts cultured with osteoblastic medium and in renal papillary tissue with Randall's plaque. A binding relationship between homeobox protein MSX-2 (MSX2) and miR-410-3p was confirmed through dual-luciferase reporter gene analysis. miR-410-3p could target MSX-2 to inhibit the osteogenic transformation of renal interstitial fibroblasts. Bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2) has been reported to be a classical phenotypic molecule during osteogenic transformation. It has been reported that lncRNA NEAT1 may act as a key activator of BMP2, thus promoting the osteogenic differentiation of renal interstitial fibroblasts. In the cytoplasm, NEAT1 sponges miR-129-5p to stabilize BMP2 mRNA. In the nucleus, NEAT1 induces the nucleolar translocation of early growth response protein 1 (EGR1), which then binds to the promotor of BMP2 and promotes its transcription. The expression of LncRNA MALAT1 was also found to be increased in human renal papillary tissue with Randall's plaque. miR-320a-5p could bind to the 3'-UTR of both MALAT1 and runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2). MALAT1 acted as a sponge of miR-320a-5p to promote Runx2 expression, thus upregulating the expression of osteogenesis-associated proteins in renal interstitial fibroblasts.
Other roles

compared the serum and urinary levels of miR-155 between 60 patients with nephrolithiasis and 50 healthy volunteers. They found that both serum and urinary levels of miR-155 were significantly higher in nephrolithiasis patients. They observed a positive correlation between plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) levels and urinary miR-155 levels. Additionally, the urinary expression of IL-1beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha showed an inverse correlation with urinary miR-155 levels. explored the exact role of miR-155 in stone formation. Similarly, they found that serum and renal levels of miR-155 were elevated in patients with CaOx stones. PI3K and Rheb were identified as downstream targets of miR-155. They ultimately showed that miR-155 facilitated CaOx crystal-induced renal tubular epithelial cell injury through PI3K-mediated autophagy. reported that miR-20b-3p was decreased in the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats and in the urine of CaOx stone patients. Treatment with miR-20b-3p-enriched exosomes protected renal function in CaOx nephrocalcinosis rats. In vitro experiments confirmed that miR-20b-3p-enriched exosomes could alleviate oxalate-induced autophagy and crystal adhesions in renal tubular epithelial cells by targeting autophagy protein 7 (ATG7) and TLR4. and reported that CaOx crystals could suppress the expression of miR-22-3p and miR-141-3p in renal tubular epithelial cells, leading to the activation of NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis. This, in turn, promoted cell injury and crystal adhesion. In addition, the lncRNA LINC00339 was upregulated in HK-2 cells treated with COM and could sponge miR-22-3p. reported that miR-21 was elevated in the renal tissue and urine of patients with CaOx stones. miR-21 promoted CaOx-induced apoptosis and lipid accumulation in renal tubular cells by targeting peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARA). demonstrated that miR-34a could inhibit the expression of the adhesion molecule CD44 to reduce COM adhesions to renal tubular epithelial cells. The expression of LncRNA CHCHD4P4 was upregulated in the renal tissue of CaOx nephrocalcinosis mice. This change promoted epithelial-mesenchymal transition in CaOx-induced renal damage. demonstrated that lncRNA LINC01197 played an inhibitory role in stone formation by sponging miR-516b-5p and subsequently activating the SIRT3/FOXO1 signaling pathway. An overview of dysregulated ncRNAs in kidney stone disease is shown in Table 2.
Dysregulated ncRNAs in kidney stone disease.

Conclusion

The role of ncRNAs in kidney stone disease has attracted much attention in recent years, offering novel perspectives to the pathogenesis of nephrolithiasis. NcRNAs can influence stone formation by regulating ion transportation, oxidative stress, inflammation, osteoblastic transformation, autophagy, and pyroptosis (Figure 3). Among the myriad dysregulated ncRNAs, we found that miR-155 was the focus of three different studies. MiR-155 is encoded by the miR-155 host gene (mir155 hg), which produces miR-155-3p and miR-155-5p forms. MiR-155 is strongly implicated in inflammatory autoimmune diseases. Drugs targeting miR-155 have been designed to treat T cell cutaneous lymphoma and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in preclinical trials. In terms of kidney stone disease, in vitro and animal studies suggest that miR-155 plays a lithogenic role by promoting CaOx-induced renal injury. The expression of miR-155 is upregulated not only in renal tubular epithelial cells cultured with CaOx but also in the renal tissue, serum, and urine from kidney stone patients. Therefore, can miR-155 serve as a reliable diagnostic and therapeutic target for nephrolithiasis? Well-designed prospective studies with an adequate number of kidney stone patients are expected to answer this question.

passages.text: Perspectives

Developing diagnostic and therapeutic methods related to ncRNAs holds great promise for precision medicine and personalized healthcare. Commonly employed strategies include identifying differential ncRNAs for early detection and monitoring of diseases, synthetizing antisense oligonucleotides to specifically inhibit the function of ncRNAs, developing effective delivery systems to enhance the bioavailability of ncRNAs, constructing small molecules to target specific ncRNA-protein interactions or ncRNA secondary structures, and using CRISPR-Cas9 system to precisely edit the genomic sequences encoding ncRNAs. These methods make the clinical application of ncRNA-based diagnosis and therapeutics in urolithiasis possible.

It is important to acknowledge that the majority of existing findings concerning nephrolithiasis-related ncRNAs come from cell and animal experiments, with limited studies conducted in patient populations. Although some studies have identified differential ncRNAs between kidney stone patients and healthy populations, the sample size is often small, and the diagnostic or therapeutic value of these ncRNAs has not been further confirmed using follow-up data. Moreover, the reported ncRNAs lack specificity, as they have also been implicated in other diseases. The stability of ncRNAs associated with nephrolithiasis has also not been thoroughly discussed either. These limitations currently hinder the application of ncRNAs in the diagnosis and treatment of kidney stone disease. It is anticipated that with future advances in research, ncRNAs can be used as reliable biomarkers or therapeutic targets in kidney stone disease.

passages.text: Influence of Treatment Effect Modifiers in Fabry Disease: A Systematic Literature Review
Objectives

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare metabolic disorder which presents with considerable heterogeneity in disease characteristics. Given the absence of interventional studies comparing all available treatments, it is important for indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) to account for potential treatment effect modifiers (TEMs). This systematic literature review (SLR) aimed to identify patient characteristics that may impact clinical outcomes by analyzing real-world evidence (RWE) in FD.
Methods

An SLR was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines, with searches performed in the EMBASE, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases (1946-2022; with a recent update in April 2023). Full-text articles reporting clinical outcomes from RWE studies of pharmacological therapies for the treatment of FD were included.
Results

Including studies from the recent SLR update, a total of 119 original studies met the PICOS criteria and 25 studies provided insights into TEMS. Potential TEMs in FD were identified: sex, age, timing of treatment initiation (early/delayed), left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria, presence of anti-drug-antibodies (ADAs) at baseline, and previous enzyme replacement therapy (ERT). In three studies (two including ERT-treated patients and one study of migalastat-treated patients) males showed worse renal outcomes than females. Five studies found that younger patients and those who received initial ERT before the age of 25 years had greater reductions in plasma-lysoGb3, as well as more favorable renal, cardiac, and biochemical outcomes. Seven studies identified associations between LVH and reduced eGFR at baseline, along with an increased risk of cardiovascular, renal, and neurological events. In four studies, lower baseline eGFR and proteinuria were associated with faster annual eGFR decline despite ERT; high baseline proteinuria was a significant predictor of renal disease progression. Baseline ADAs were linked to lower eGFR, increased left ventricular mass, and reduced treatment impact on plasma/urine-lysoGb3. Migalastat was effective in treatment-naive patients, while those previously treated with ERT experienced deteriorations in mean lysoGb3, eGFR, and left ventricular mass.
Conclusions
This SLR highlighted several patient characteristics that influence treatment effectiveness in FD. It is important to account for these characteristics in ITCs to ensure unbiased outcomes.
Key Summary Points

infons.xml:
Our study found that certain traits in patients with Fabry disease might influence treatment effectiveness.
Patient features including male sex, classic disease type, reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate, baseline level of antibodies against the drug, or baseline left ventricular hypertrophy were linked to negative results, whereas early initiation of treatment in young patients showed positive effects.
Understanding the influence of the patient traits can inform effective management decisions for patients with Fabry disease, ultimately improving the quality of life.

Introduction

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare X-linked inherited lysosomal storage disorder characterized by pathogenic variants in the galactosidase alpha (GLA) gene, resulting in a deficiency of the alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-Gal A) enzyme. This enzymatic deficiency leads to the progressive lysosomal accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), globotriaosylsphingosine (lysoGb3), and related glycolipids in various cells and tissues, ranging from the autonomic nervous system, dorsal root ganglia, and kidney epithelial cells, to cells in the vascular system and myocardium.

FD can be divided into a classical phenotype, most often seen in men without residual enzyme activity (< 1%), and a generally milder nonclassical or late-onset phenotype in patients with significant residual alpha-Gal A activity. The onset of symptoms in classical FD begins in childhood or adolescence and includes the characteristic FD symptoms, such as neuropathic pain, corneal and lenticular opacities (cornea verticillate), cutaneous vascular lesions (angiokeratoma), and abnormalities in sweating (anhidrosis, hypohidrosis, and hyperhidrosis). Long-term manifestations can also include cardiomyopathy, progressive kidney failure, stroke, chronic pain, hearing loss, and gastrointestinal issues, all of which severely affect patients' quality of life (QoL). Late-onset FD can have a more variable disease course and symptoms tend to appear in adulthood and could be restricted to a single organ. Nevertheless, these patients may also develop severe symptoms such as Fabry cardiomyopathy or nephropathy. Given the X-linked inheritance pattern, heterozygous women tend to have less severe manifestations than men; however, given the random X chromosomal inactivation, FD manifestations in females can vary widely, from being asymptomatic to exhibiting severe manifestations akin to those seen in males.

In younger (teenage) patients with FD, angiokeratomas and proteinuria (a marker of kidney disease) may typically be detected and might begin to experience gastrointestinal distress. As patients with FD grow older, they could be at significant risk of cardiovascular disease (left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, valvular disease), deterioration of renal function leading to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), cerebrovascular disease (ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack) and nephropathy. Patients may develop osteopenia/osteoporosis, experience neuropathic pain, and exhibit neuropsychiatric phenotype. However, it is important to note that the clinical manifestations of the disease are heterogeneous, and that the impact of treatment can vary based on factors such as age, sex, disease severity, genetic profile/phenotype, and age at initiation of treatment. Therapeutic goals aim to address the multifaceted challenges posed by FD, including alleviating symptoms, preventing or slowing the progression of organ damage, and enhancing patients' QoL, ultimately working towards normalizing life expectancy.

Current therapeutic options for FD include enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and chaperone therapy. ERT replaces the missing or deficient alpha-Gal A activity with recombinant human alpha-Gal A that reduces substrate accumulation. Chaperone therapy is indicated only in patients with amenable genetic variants as it binds and stabilizes misfolded alpha-Gal A, improving its transportation and accumulation in lysosomes. Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) is a new treatment modality in the most advanced stages of development for FD and acts by inhibiting the enzyme involved in the production of Gb3 precursors and ultimately reducing the accumulation of Gb3 in the cell.

There are currently three ERTs available: agalsidase alfa [Replagal , licensed dose 0.2 mg/kg every other week (EOW)] is approved in Canada, Europe, Japan, and Australia; agalsidase beta [Fabrazyme , licensed dose 1.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks (E2W)] is approved in the US, Europe, Canada, Japan, and Australia; and pegunigalsidase alfa (Elfabrio ; licensed dose 1 mg/kg EOW), a pegylated form of an alpha-Gal ERT offering a long half-life (ranging from 53 to 134 h) was recently approved in the US and Europe. Migalastat (Galafold ) is an alpha-Gal A molecular chaperone for patients with FD with an amenable GLA variant that was approved in various countries including the US, Canada, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

While there are currently four treatment options available for FD, as indicated above, data comparing their efficacy are scarce. The pivotal studies of agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta included placebo-controlled trials but did not include an active control arm. Of the two pivotal studies of migalastat, one included a placebo comparator arm, whereas the other included an active comparator arm of ERT (either agalsidase alfa or beta). The approval of pegunigalsidase alfa was based on one head-to-head study comparing pegunigalsidase alfa to agalsidase beta and two switch-over studies from ERT (agalsidase alfa and/or beta) to pegunigalsidase alfa. This was the first head-to-head study in FD and directly compared pegunigalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta in patients with deteriorating renal function who had previously been treated with agalsidase beta (>= 1 year). Although some other studies have directly compared agalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta, those were not randomized interventional trials. Furthermore, while meta-analyses, indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs), and propensity score matching studies have also been conducted in FD, an ITC comparing all therapies has not been conducted to our knowledge. Within the current landscape, a notable gap exists in published interventional studies directly comparing treatments for FD. This absence underscores the need for a comprehensive evaluation of the treatment effect modifiers (TEMs), which can be effectively addressed through ITCs. These comparative analyses serve as an important tool to offer insights into the relative effectiveness of all interventions. To ensure the robustness and unbiased reporting of indirect treatment comparisons, the identification and consideration of TEMs is paramount. These modifiers may significantly influence treatment responses and hence, the validity of the results.
The objective of this study was to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) of real-world evidence (RWE) in FD to identify TEMs that may impact clinical outcomes.
Methods

SLR searches were conducted using the Ovid platform with a time restriction of 1946 through to the search date of 1 August 2022, and a recent update was conducted on 12 April 2023 (search period: 1 August 2022 to 12 April 2023). The databases searched included Ovid MEDLINE ALL, Embase, Econlit, and Cochrane databases for full-text articles reporting clinical outcomes of RWE studies on pharmacological therapies for the treatment of FD. The SLR adhered to established guidance and methods as described by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and Centre for Reviews and Dissemination.

aWhile lucerastat and venglustat were included in the initial SLR search strategy, they were later excluded as these drugs are still under development

This SLR included adult patients diagnosed with FD who received one or more of the following interventions: agalsidase alfa, agalsidase beta, migalastat, and pegunigalsidase alfa. Multiple study designs were considered for inclusion, including prospective observational studies, retrospective studies, registry analyses, database analyses, non-interventional studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, ITCs, and pooled analyses based on RWE. Real-world studies reporting on effectiveness outcomes, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), lysoGb3 levels, left ventricular mass index (LMVI), cardiovascular (CV) events, renal events, urinary protein to creatinine ratio (UP/Cr), survival, and safety were considered for inclusion (Table 1). Data extraction was conducted by a single reviewer, followed by an independent quality check by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies were resolved by a third reviewer, ensuring data accuracy and consistency.

This analysis is based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors and the data are not identifiable. Further the data from the databases used in the searches are not identifiable. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required for this study. The systematic literature review used publicly available databases.

A total of 940 publications were identified in the original SLR conducted in August 2022. A recent SLR search conducted on 12 April 2023 resulted in the retrieval of 11 additional articles, of which four reported TEMs (Table 2). With the recent update, a total of 119 original studies that met the PICOS criteria and 25 studies reporting on TEMs were selected for inclusion (Fig. 1). Several TEMs in FD were identified from studies included in the SLR, including early ERT initiation (defined as ERT initiated in younger patients (< 25 years old) or ERT initiated within 2 years of symptoms/diagnosis), sex, baseline left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), reduced eGFR, prior ERT and migalastat treatment, presence of antidrug antibodies (ADAs), and baseline proteinuria. The studies identified in the SLR that reported on TEMs in FD are described in Table 2.
Prompt Versus Delayed ERT Initiation

Five studies found that patients who initiated ERT early at a younger age (i.e., < 25 years) presented with better biomarker responses to ERT than those who initiated treatment later at an older age (i.e., >= 25 years). In addition, early treatment initiation within 2 years of symptoms or of a diagnosis, resulted in more favorable renal, cardiac, and biomarker outcomes. One study highlighted that males who started treatment before the age of 25 years (early) were seven times more likely to achieve a lysoGb3 level of < 20 nmol/L compared with males who started treatment aged 25 years or above (late) [adjusted odds ratios (OR) of 7.38; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.91 to 34.04, p = 0.006]. Adjusted lysoGb3 levels in male patients 1 year after ERT initiation were 12.9 nmol/L lower in the early treatment group versus the late treatment group (95% CI - 20.1 to - 5.8, p < 0.001). Another study found that initiating ERT within 24 months of symptom onset was linked to a significantly lower risk of a CV [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.62, p < 0.001] and renal event (HR = 0.57, p < 0.001) compared with delayed ERT initiation (24 months or later). Similarly, prompt ERT initiation within 24 months of diagnosis was associated with a significantly lower risk of CV events (HR = 0.83; p = 0.003) compared with delayed initiation (24 months or later), although it did not affect the risk of renal events (HR = 0.96, p = 0.563).
Sex

From two studies, differences in renal outcomes were evident based on sex in patients treated with ERT, with male patients presenting with worse renal outcomes than female patients in ERT-treated patients. A study examined the impact of sex on eGFR change over a decade in patients treated with agalsidase alfa, specifically those with a baseline eGFR >= 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. This study reported that, in female patients (n = 52, median age at treatment start 48.8 years), the mean eGFR slope (95% CI) remained relatively stable at - 0.55 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (- 1.12 to 0.01), whereas, in male patients (n = 79, median age at treatment start 34.4 years), there was a slight decline at - 1.99 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (95% CI - 2.45 to - 1.54). Additionally, a linear disease progression model based on data from 98 classic phenotype ERT-treated patients, estimated a decline in eGFR for males (median baseline eGFR = 96 mL/min/1.73 m2) but not for females (median baseline eGFR = 92 mL/min/1.73 m2), with eGFR slopes of - 3.07 versus - 0.07 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year, respectively. In this study, participants started ERT at comparable median ages, with females having commenced ERT at 36 (range 21-54) years and males at 39 (range 28-49) years of age. Furthermore, a prospective 24-month observational study in patients treated with migalastat, reported a lower mean eGFR decline in 2 years in females versus males (mean eGFR of - 5.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 vs. - 8.9 mL/min/1.73 m2 within 24 months, respectively).
Phenotype

The classic phenotype in patients with FD has been linked to notable clinical outcomes including eGFR regression, risk of renal transplantation, and higher lysoGb3 levels. In an analysis of the prospective French FABRY cohort, males with the classic phenotype were significantly associated with eGFR regression (p = 0.008), an increased risk of requiring renal transplantation (HR = 7.9, p = 0.005), and markedly higher lysoGb3 levels (median of 21.1 ng/mL vs. 4.5 ng/mL, p = 0.0005) compared with those with the non-classic phenotype.
Baseline LVH

Six studies identified that having baseline LVH poses an increased risk of CV events among patients undergoing ERT. A retrospective analysis of the Fabry Outcome Survey (FOS) provided further insights. It demonstrated that, in a subgroup of patients with LVH compared with those with normal left ventricular mass index (LVMI) at baseline, the risk for a CV event was significantly higher (HR = 1.57; 95% CI 1.21-2.05; p < 0.001). However, the risk for a renal event showed no significant difference between the two subgroups (HR = 1.90; 95% CI 0.94-3.85; p = 0.074). Further, higher LVMI was associated with an increased risk of developing adverse clinical events (HR = 2.21; 95% CI 1.43-3.42; p < 0.001). For LVMI per 10 g/m2.7, the risk of an adverse event increased by 25% (HR = 1.25; 95% CI 1.08-1.45; p < 0.01).
Reduced eGFR

Impaired baseline renal function was identified from seven studies as an important predictor for greater risk of clinical events; these included CV, renal, and neurological events, as well as a faster annual decline in eGFR in patients undergoing ERT. Graziani et al. reported a Cox regression HR of 0.97 (p = 0.008) for major clinical events associated with eGFR modification of diet in renal diet (MDRD). The retrospective analysis from the FOS showed that patients with a low eGFR at baseline (< 90 mL/min/1.73 m2) had a significantly higher risk for both a CV event (HR = 1.33; 95% CI 1.04-1.70; p = 0.021) and a renal event (HR = 5.88; 95% CI 2.73-12.68; p < 0.001) compared with those with a normal eGFR at baseline (>= 90 mL/min/1.73 m2). Furthermore, an eGFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 was linked to a three- to seven-fold increase in the risk of clinical events, as indicated by different Cox regression models. In a separate retrospective analysis of ERT-naive patients from 2002 to 2016, baseline eGFR levels of less than 75 mL/min/1.73 m2 were associated with a more than threefold increase in the risk of CV events (HR = 3.59; p = 0.0273) and a nearly fivefold increase in the risk of combined CV, renal, and neurological events (HR = 4.77; p = 0.0007) while receiving ERT. Further, another study based on a univariate or multivariate Cox regression analysis showed that lower eGFR at baseline was associated with an increased risk of developing an adverse clinical event (HR = 0.41; 95% CI 0.27-0.62; p < 0.001).
Proteinuria

The UP/Cr ratio was identified as the most significant indicator of renal disease progression, particularly in adult patients, as highlighted in four separate retrospective analyses of registry data in patients treated with ERT. In one study, patients experiencing rapid renal disease progression, as evidenced by a decline in eGFR, had significantly higher mean UP/Cr levels compared with those with slower renal disease progression (1.5 vs. 0.2 for men; 1.4 vs. 0.5 for women; p < 0.0001). Similarly, in another study, baseline UP/Cr ratio exceeding 1 g/g was strongly associated with rapid renal disease progression compared with those with a baseline UP/Cr below 0.3 g/g (OR = 112; 95% CI 4-3109; p = 0.0054). In two studies, patients treated with ERT had high baseline proteinuria presenting faster eGFR decline compared to patients with low baseline proteinuria.
Prior ERT and Migalastat Treatment

One study indicated that the clinical benefits of migalastat were more pronounced in ERT-naive patients than in those with prior ERT experience. In a retrospective analysis conducted over a 12-month follow-up period of patients receiving migalastat treatment, eGFR in the ERT-naive group (n = 33) remained stable over the study period (mean eGFR at initiation: 82 mL/min; mean eGFR at 12 months: 81.2 mL/min). Conversely, a slight decline in eGFR was observed in the prior-ERT group (n = 44) (mean eGFR at initiation: 81 mL/min; mean eGFR at 12 months: 77.2 mL/min). Furthermore, left ventricular mass in the ERT-naive group declined from 128.9 g/m2 at treatment initiation to 117.2 g/m2 at 12 months, whereas it remained relatively stable in the prior ERT group (initiation: 113.6 g/m2; at 12 months: 115.9 g/m2). It is important to note that these changes are small and correspond to a small number of patients treated with migalastat in a RWE study. At baseline, ERT-naive patients had higher left ventricular mass than those with prior ERT experience (128.9 g/m2 vs. 113.6 g/m2). Patients in this study do not reflect the overall FD population given migalastat is used only FD patients with amenable genetic variants.
ADAs

Antidrug antibodies can develop towards ERTs and may have neutralizing/inhibitory capacity against the ERT. Presence of ADAs has been associated with higher left ventricular mass and greater reduction in renal function compared with patients without ADAs. In a multivariate regression analysis of 68 male patients (2001-2014), those with serum-mediated ERT inhibition had higher left ventricular mass compared to those without ERT inhibition (105.8 g/m2 vs. 71.5 g/m2; p = 0.02). Correspondingly, eGFR was significantly decreased in patients with serum-mediated ERT inhibition compared to those without it (eGFR, ml/min per 1.73 m2: 64.1 vs. 93.3; p = 0.04). In a 5-year longitudinal analysis, presence of ERT inhibition was associated with severely decreased renal function (p = 0.03). Another retrospective study employing a linear mixed effect model reported that ERT inhibition-positive male patients (n = 39) receiving ERT had an accelerated decline in renal function of approximately 1.2 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year compared to those without inhibition (p = 0.042). Further, 14 patients who had ADA saturation (and therefore unbound ERT after infusion) experienced a mild reduction in eGFR (- 3.0 mL/min per 1.73 m2) and stable ventricular septum thickness (0.2 mm/year), whereas patients who have saturated ERT and excess ADAs after infusions had a greater reduction in eGFR (- 4.8 mL/min per 1.73 m2) and increased ventricular septum thickness (0.4 mm/year).

Presence of ADAs may also impact plasma levels of the FD biomarker lysoGb3. Patients who developed ADAs experienced smaller reductions in both plasma lysoGb3 and urinary Gb3 levels than patients without ADAs. In a prospective observational study spanning a 6-year ERT follow-up period, the decline in plasma lysoGb3 from baseline was significantly less pronounced in males with ADAs (n = 12) in comparison with males without ADAs (n = 11) (p < 0.043). Among male patients without ADAs, urinary Gb3 levels decreased markedly from baseline in the first year of ERT treatment and remained low through year 6 (range 19-387 nmol/24 h; p = 0.028). Conversely, male patients with ADAs showed no significant reduction in urinary Gb3 levels during the first year (p = 0.79), with levels remaining elevated over 8 years of treatment (range 216-4547 nmol/24 h). Furthermore, in a separate prospective study, patients who tested positive for ADAs, had a significantly higher frequency of dialysis or renal transplantation than ADA-negative patients (33.3% vs. 3.7%; p = 0.012).

Discussion

Previous studies reported that FD continues to impose a significant QoL and health utility burden which are often influenced by sex, age, disease severity and complications, and treatment status. In this present study, we conducted an SLR to identify patient characteristics/TEMs that may impact clinical outcomes of pharmacological therapies for the treatment of FD. Among 119 original articles, those identified as having a potential negative impact on clinical outcomes included male sex, classic FD phenotype, LVH at baseline, reduced eGFR at baseline (a measure of renal function), presence of proteinuria at baseline, prior ERT and migalastat treatment, and presence of ADAs at baseline. We found in two studies of ERT-treated and one study of migalastat-treated patients that males had poorer renal outcomes than females. Four studies reported that reduced eGFR and proteinuria were linked to faster annual eGFR decline despite ERT treatment and that high baseline proteinuria was a significant indicator of renal disease progression. Additionally, seven studies reported a correlation between LVH and reduced eGFR at baseline, and increased risk of cardiovascular, renal, and neurological events. Our findings align with studies such as Hanneman et al., which highlighted that a 5-g/m2 increase in LVMI was associated with an 8% more likelihood of experiencing an adverse cardiac event. Further, the risk of adverse cardiac event was three times higher in patients with LVM than those without LVH (HR = 3.0; 95% CI 1.1-8.11; p = 0.03). Spinelli et al. conducted a receiver operative characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and established an LVMI threshold of 54.3 g/h2.7 for the prediction of a cardiac event, suggesting the association of LVMI > 54.3 g/h2.7 with cardiac events. LVH was identified as the significant predictor of adverse cardiac outcome (HR = 1.022; p < 0.002).

Additionally, the ROC curve analysis identified a predictive eGFR threshold at 69 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating the association of eGFR < 69 mL/min/1.73 m2 with cardiac events and eGFR was identified as the significant predictor of adverse cardiac outcome (HR = 0.98; p = 0.016). Consistent with our findings, Patel et al. reported higher odds of CV events for individuals with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (OR = 2.33; 95% CI 1.22-4.45; p < 0.05 for men, OR = 3.85; 95% CI 1.78-8.32; p < 0.0001 for women); the odds were higher for women. Furthermore, presence of ADAs at baseline was associated with a reduced treatment effect on plasma/urine-lysoGb3. Moreover, in the context of migalastat treatment, a positive effect was observed in treatment-naive patients, whereas patients with prior ERT demonstrated deteriorations in mean lysoGb3, eGFR, and left ventricular mass.

Early initiation of ERT was identified as a TEM with a positive effect on treatment outcomes. Five studies found that patients who initiated ERT early and at a young age (before the age of 25 years) experienced greater reductions in plasma-lysoGb3, and more favorable renal, cardiac, and biochemical outcomes, than those starting treatment at a later age (>= 25 years).

In the expanding treatment landscape of FD, the availability of comparative evidence regarding the relative effectiveness of available treatment options is essential to healthcare decision-making and health technology assessments. While randomized controlled trials are regarded as the gold standard for establishing efficacy, conducting head-to-head trials with multiple relevant comparators is not always feasible. In such circumstances, leveraging ITCs is a key approach to gaining valuable insights. In addition to ERT and chaperone therapy options, there are several emerging therapies in FD, including substrate reduction and gene therapies, suggesting that additional new treatment options may be added to the treatment landscape in the future.

While only one head-to-head study comparing pegunigalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta is available, many pivotal studies, including the landmark therapies such as migalastat versus ERT, pegunigalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta, and agalsidase alfa versus beta, have been either placebo-controlled or switch studies. Data have been published from the Canadian Fabry Disease Initiative (CFDI) comparing agalsidase alfa and beta, which found no difference between the two types of ERT on a composite endpoint that included renal, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular events, or death. Other comparative studies either did not use the licensed dose of agalsidase beta or pooled findings of the two ERT formulations.

Findings from meta-analyses, ITCs, and propensity score matching studies conducted in FD have identified heterogeneity between FD studies regarding patient populations included, disease stage, inclusion criteria, and endpoints assessed. Consistent with findings in our study, two meta-analyses identified early initiation of therapy, age, sex, and proteinuria (as a measure of renal function) as being covariates that potentially influenced treatment outcomes. Of note, these ITCs and meta-analyses were specific to certain treatments (i.e., switching from agalsidase alfa to beta, ERT (agalsidase alfa beta), eGFR in studies of agalsidase beta, and did not compare all available treatment options.

Consequently, there is a lack of published studies that directly compare all available treatment options and their licensed doses. Comparative effectiveness analyses using ITCs are therefore important to assess the relative efficacy of different therapies in FD. To ensure the robustness of these comparisons, it is important to employ rigorous statistical methodologies that adequately address potential baseline differences in patient characteristics. The standard approach for ITCs and network meta-analyses use aggregate data from studies and assumes that the distribution of patient characteristics that can influence the effect of treatment (effect-modifying variables) are the same between studies. Methods that adjust for differences between trials in the distribution of covariates in patient populations using individual patient-level data (IPD) are becoming increasingly common in health technology assessment submissions to agencies such as the NICE. These methods include matched-adjusted indirect comparisons, which reduce bias in comparative effectiveness assessments by adjusting for TEMs. This is particularly relevant in FD given the considerable variation in patient characteristics, disease phenotypes (i.e., early vs. late onset), and clinical manifestations of disease in terms of symptom presentation, organ involvement, and severity of disease. Moreover, treatment guidelines in FD highlight that the clinical effects of disease-specific therapy vary based on individual patient characteristics and disease phenotype and recommend tailoring treatment goals to the individual patient.

Our study did have a few limitations which are important to acknowledge. Given that this was an SLR of RWE focusing on a rare disease, the studies we identified typically involved small patient numbers and may not have been entirely representative of the broader FD population due to missing data. This is a common challenge faced in other meta-analyses of rare diseases. Furthermore, in most studies, patient selection was not conducted via randomization, and, in the case of registry studies, relied on patient enrollment that may have introduced selection bias. Additionally, the varying duration of follow-up across the identified studies may have affected the precision of our findings.
Conclusion

Although this SLR identified several patient characteristics as TEMs that may influence treatment effectiveness in FD, their impacts were mixed: some had a positive effect, while others had a negative effect. Patient characteristics including male sex, classic FD phenotype, and baseline LVH, among others, were identified as TEMs with a potentially negative impact on outcomes. In contrast, early initiation of ERT was a positive TEM that had a beneficial effect. Adjustments for these should be considered during indirect treatment comparisons to reduce bias.

passages.text: Effects of Current Therapies on Disease Progression in Fabry Disease: A Narrative Review for Better Patient Management in Clinical Practice

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare lysosomal storage disorder that is characterized by renal, neurological, and cardiovascular dysfunction. Four treatments are currently available for patients with FD; three enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs; agalsidase alfa, agalsidase beta, and pegunigalsidase alfa) and one pharmacological chaperone (migalastat). This review focuses on the evidence for the benefits of ERTs and migalastat, and provides an overview of their impact on disease manifestations and quality of life (QoL). Agalsidase beta is associated with renal, neurological, and cardiovascular benefits, and may prevent renal disease progression. Agalsidase alfa provides stabilizing effects across all main organ systems, although minor sex-specific differences exist in patients with more advanced baseline disease. The benefits of agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta are similar but depend on the extent of baseline disease. Some data indicate that agalsidase beta may be preferable over the longer term. Both agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta are associated with improved gastrointestinal and pain symptoms, as well as improved QoL. Patients with advanced end-organ damage tend not to respond as optimally to ERTs as those who initiate ERTs before irreversible organ fibrosis develops, highlighting the need for early treatment initiation. Migalastat, which is only approved for patients with amenable missense gene variants, generally stabilizes renal parameters and provides cardiovascular benefits. Migalastat also improves diarrhea and pain, and stabilizes QoL (although ERT may be more effective for pain management), but the neurological effects of migalastat have not been studied. Real-world data raise concerns about effective in vivo amenability of some genetic variants. Future studies with direct treatment comparisons in patients with FD are needed.

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare lysosomal storage disorder that is characterized by renal, neurological, and cardiovascular dysfunction.
Treatments available for patients with FD include enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs; agalsidase beta, agalsidase alfa, and pegunigalsidase alfa) and a pharmacological chaperone (migalastat).
The benefits of agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta are similar but depend on the extent of baseline disease.
Migalastat is only approved in patients with an amenable alpha-galactosidase mutation, and generally stabilizes renal parameters and provides cardiovascular benefits, although real-world data raise concerns about the effective in vivo amenability of some genetic variants.
Despite the therapeutic benefits of available options, no treatments can considerably reverse the major organ damage caused by FD progression.

Introduction

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare, X-linked, lysosomal storage disorder that results from deficient alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-Gal A) activity caused by a variant of the alpha-galactosidase (GLA) gene, with a prevalence estimated at around 1 in 40,000-170,000 births. FD presents in both males and females; however, there is a wide spectrum of disease severity.

Two FD phenotypes have been described, the 'classical', with earlier onset, rapid disease progression and severe outcomes, and the 'non-classical' or 'late-onset' FD. Although the extent of the non-classical phenotype may be initially less when compared to the classical disease presentation, the severity of individual renal or cardiac manifestations in advanced stages of patients with late-onset variants may be significant enough to require renal replacement therapy or pacemaker/cardioverter defibrillator implantation. Males with the classical phenotype typically have no residual alpha-Gal A activity versus males with the non-classical phenotype, where residual alpha-Gal A activity may be present even if below the normal range. Comparatively, females with GLA pathogenic variants may have normal or only slightly reduced alpha-Gal A activity and so generally have a milder disease course. However, females can also show a range of disease severity, from asymptomatic to symptomatic with severe organ involvement. The differences in male and female disease phenotypes can be explained by the random inactivation of the X chromosome in heterozygous females (known as lyonization), which is dependent on the cell type and is frequently nonuniform across the silenced chromosome.

Numerous variants of the GLA gene are responsible for the development of FD, with few variants presenting recurrently. Of the GLA variants identified through genomic screening, both pathogenic and non-pathogenic variants have been found. Some of the identified variants have been classified as variants of unknown significance (VUS), indicating that, at present, the genetic changes underlying those variants have no validated association with the corresponding phenotype or inconsistent phenotypes. The substantial genotypic variability of FD underlies considerable phenotypic heterogeneity, which makes FD diagnosis especially challenging, particularly in the case of a VUS.

The pathophysiological mechanisms of FD have not yet been fully elucidated; however, the absence of alpha-Gal A activity determines a pathological lysosomal accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) and/or its metabolite globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-GL-3) within lysosome-containing tissues. The accumulation of GL-3 and lyso-GL-3 is considered to be the main mechanism leading to cellular damage and eventually organ dysfunction. Typically, the major affected organs are the heart, kidneys, and central nervous system (CNS), and heart failure, renal failure, and stroke can result from disease progression. The pathology of FD is also thought to result from secondary functional and biochemical changes, particularly in the heart and kidneys. Tissue lyso-GL-3 deposits may trigger chronic inflammation and accelerate rates of apoptosis in many organs, including the heart and kidneys. Figure 1 demonstrates the progressive nature of this damage in the heart.

At present, four therapies are approved for the treatment of FD in the United States (US) and/or Europe: three enzyme replacement therapies [ERTs; i.e., agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme , Sanofi), agalsidase alfa (Replagal , Takeda UK), and pegunigalsidase alfa (Elfabrio , Chiesi Farmaceutici)], and one pharmacological chaperone [i.e., migalastat (Galafold , Amicus Therapeutics)].

Both agalsidase beta (approved in Europe in 2001 and in the US in 2003) and agalsidase alfa (approved in Europe in 2001, but not approved in the US) are indicated for patients with confirmed FD and prevent the accumulation of glycosphingolipids by hydrolyzing and removing GL-3. Agalsidase beta is approved for use in individuals aged >= 8 years in Europe and >= 2 years in the US, whereas in Europe, algalsidase alfa is approved for individuals aged >= 7 years. Pegunigalsidase alfa (approved in both Europe and the US in 2023) is a hydrolytic lysosomal neutral glycosphingolipid-specific enzyme indicated for the treatment of adults with confirmed FD that has a prolonged plasma half-life compared with other available ERTs. Migalastat (approved in Europe in 2017 for adults and adolescents aged >= 16 and extended to patients aged >= 12 years in 2021, but not reimbursed in the Netherlands, and approved in the US for use in adults, in 2018) reversibly and selectively binds with high affinity to the active sites of certain alpha-Gal A variants, enabling the trafficking of the variant forms to lysosomes, where migalastat disassociates and alpha-Gal A activity is restored, thereby allowing for catabolism of GL-3 and related substrates. Migalastat projected therapeutic benefit in patients with FD for particular GLA variants is based on an in vitro assay that determines amenability, which is the basis of treatment suitability. Based on this in vitro assay, it has been determined that 367 GLA variants are amenable to migalastat treatment and 711 are likely not. Migalastat is only licensed for use in patients who have amenable variants included in a list provided by Amicus Therapeutics. However, in vivo data from studies reassessing these variants' amenability in cells have shown conflicting results. Clinicians are advised to evaluate the pathogenic role of the variant and to monitor clinical manifestations and lyso-GL-3 levels to confirm that a variant is really amenable in vivo.

This narrative review focuses on the clinical evidence for the benefits of ERTs and migalastat on the three major organ systems involved in FD pathology (i.e., the renal, neurological, and cardiovascular systems) in classical and non-classical FD phenotypes, and provides a brief overview of their impact on disease manifestations and patient quality of life (QoL). The aim of this article is to help physicians across all specialties make informed decisions when prescribing therapies for FD treatment.
Data Sources and Searches

To identify relevant data, we initially conducted searches of titles and abstracts of English-language articles on the PubMed database between 24 and 28 October 2022. Search terms (along with any synonyms) included each drug name, as well as 'enzyme replacement therapy', in combination with the terms for FD and applicable MeSH terms relating to the effects of interest (e.g., neurological, nephrological, and cardiovascular). Other articles were subsequently identified through searches of the reference lists of articles identified in the database search, as well as from ad hoc searches for relevant literature, and from the authors' experience in the area. Updated and newer publications after 2022 relating to pegunigalsidase alfa were also included.
This article is based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors.
Renal Involvement in FD

Renal involvement is well documented in patients with FD, with substantial GL-3 accumulation seen in renal epithelial cells (podocytes) and glomerular and tubular epithelial cells. While the severity of nephropathy can be variable, untreated male patients tend to progress through three clinical stages. The first stage is characterized by glomerular hyperfiltration; the second by renal dysfunctions with proteinuria, Malta crystals in the urine sediment, impaired urine concentrating and diluting ability, and lipiduria; and the third by severe renal disease. The prevalence of glomerular hyperfiltration has been reported to be particularly high (50%) in younger patients with FD (<= 40 years of age). Given that progressive nephropathy is a key feature of FD, hyperfiltration may be considered an early marker of FD, as it precedes other organ-related symptoms and signs of disease. Moreover, long-term evaluation of renal function should be considered when angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are used in patients with FD because they may interfere with the evolution of renal function. Another early sign of FD in the kidneys is parapelvic cysts, which have been reported in 30% of patients with FD.

Several studies, including phase 3 trials and those assessing both adults and children with FD, have demonstratec that renal function remains stable during agalsidase beta treatment (Table 1), suggesting that agalsidase beta may help prevent pathological progression of kidney disease. In particular, follow-up data from one phase 3 trial at both 30 months and 54 months have shown sustained, long-term renal stabilization with agalsidase beta treatment in patients with FD. Various other renal benefits have also been documented with agalsidase beta (Table 1). Two studies have demonstrated significant reversal of GL-3 accumulation in renal cells with agalsidase beta. In a small prospective study of eight adults, proteinuria had resolved in five patients after 45 months of treatment with agalsidase beta.

Several studies have also suggested that agalsidase beta provides long-term renal benefits in patients with FD (Table 1). A 10-year study reported a significant decrease in mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) slope with agalsidase beta in patients with classical FD and high or low renal involvement at baseline. Similarly, Wanner and colleagues showed that female patients (with high or low renal involvement) had stable renal function over 5 years of agalsidase beta treatment. In a smaller study of 10 children with FD receiving agalsidase beta, renal stability was maintained for 8 years of follow-up; one patient with an elevated albumin-to-creatinine ratio at baseline showed normalization of renal function.

For patients with considerable renal function impairment at baseline, the benefits of agalsidase beta are not confirmed (Table 1). In one study of 82 adults with advanced FD, agalsidase beta treatment delayed the onset of a composite clinical outcome of renal, cardiovascular, and cerebrovascular events or death compared with placebo; larger treatment effects were observed in patients with baseline eGFR > 55 mL/min/1.73 m2 compared with those with a baseline eGFR <= 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. A single-center study in 26 patients with FD found that eGFR significantly decreased during agalsidase beta treatment in those with renal impairment at baseline. Notably, in that trial, although the overall population reported stable renal function, a few patients with advanced disease (including those with glomerulosclerosis) showed kidney disease progression despite receiving agalsidase beta. A pivotal phase 3 trial reported that of the six patents who had renal disease progression with agalsidase beta, all had sclerotic glomeruli and significant proteinuria at baseline. Taken together, these findings suggest that the benefits of agalsidase beta are likely dependent on the extent of disease progression at the time of treatment initiation.

Studies have found that renal function remains stable during agalsidase alfa treatment (Table 2). The renal effects of agalsidase alfa also appear to be dependent on the extent of renal impairment at treatment initiation.

A retrospective 10-year cross-sectional study in patients receiving agalsidase alfa reported a relatively stable eGFR in females with and without impaired renal function at baseline; however, males with baseline renal function impairment had a modest decline in eGFR. In a cross-sectional analysis of an open-label extension study in 25 males with FD, eGFR showed a slight decline during 4.0-4.5 years of agalsidase alfa treatment. When stratified by renal function, four patients with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) appeared to be driving the eGFR decline, with a mean decline of ~ 5.2 mL/min/1.73 m2/year. While these results suggest a sex-specific response, other findings have demonstrated that both male and female patients with FD have limited benefit with agalsidase alfa if their renal function is impaired at baseline. The Fabry Outcome Survey has investigated sex-specific differences in treatment response among patients with FD receiving agalsidase alfa. The median change in eGFR was - 1.5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year for females (similar to the general decline expected due to aging) and - 2.1 mL/min/1.73 m2/year for males. Among patients who had an eGFR decrease of >= 10% according to the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease formula, there was a greater proportion of males than females with worsened renal function.

The importance of renal function at baseline was confirmed in a study of female patients with FD who had been receiving agalsidase alfa for 4 years. Renal function remained relatively stable in the overall population; however, patients with moderate renal disease at baseline had a significant and sustained improvement over 1 year of treatment. In contrast, four patients with hyperfiltration at baseline experienced an eGFR decline.

Alternatively, a long-term open-label study has shown an improved slope of eGFR decline with more frequent agalsidase alfa treatment. The study examined 11 male patients who had participated in long-term agalsidase alfa clinical trials and who had a slope of eGFR decline of >= 5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year while receiving long-term agalsidase alfa 0.2 mg/kg every other week (EOW). Before switching to weekly dosing, the mean +- standard error of the mean eGFR was 53.7 +- 6.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 and the mean rate of change in eGFR was - 8.0 +- 0.8 mL/min/1.73 m2/year. After switching to weekly dosing, over the course of the 24-month follow-up period the mean rate of change in eGFR slowed to - 3.3 +- 1.4 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (P < 0.01 compared with EOW), demonstrating an improved slope of decline when the same dose was given more frequently.

Overall, these findings suggest that the renal system is stabilized with agalsidase alfa when treatment is initiated in patients with stage 1-2 CKD; however, the benefits are less apparent in those with stage >= 3 CKD, for whom a minor sex-specific difference in treatment response may occur.
Comparative Effects of Agalsidase Beta Versus Agalsidase Alfa

Data directly comparing agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta are limited; however, various noncomparative and retrospective studies have been performed and demonstrated the value of both agents in improving renal function in patients with FD, with some studies suggesting a difference in treatment effectiveness.

A systematic review compared the efficacy and safety of ERT in patients with FD using a linear regression and pooled analysis. When one study assessing agalsidase beta was compared with six studies of agalsidase alfa (which had significant heterogeneity), there were no significant differences between the treatments with regards to renal complications. However, a significant difference in renal impairment was seen between patients treated with agalsidase beta and untreated patients (in 11 studies), emphasizing the importance of initiating ERT to prevent renal disease. Similarly, a retrospective study that directly compared agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta reported no significant differences in eGFR slope, regardless of whether eGFR was < 60 or >= 60 mL/min/1.73 m2.

A head-to-head study by Vedder and colleagues comparing the same dose of agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta (0.2 mg/kg EOW; i.e., an unlicensed dose of agalsidase beta) reported no differences in renal function. This study also assessed treatment failure, defined as renal disease progression (either a 33% increase in serum creatinine or requirement for dialysis or transplantation), cardiac disease progression (heart failure requiring hospitalization, a new infarction, or the need for cardioversion or anti-arrhythmic drugs), or a neurologist-diagnosed new cerebrovascular accident or new lacunar infarctions identified on magnetic resonance imaging by an experienced neuroradiologist. Of note, treatment failure due to renal insufficiency (> 33% increase in serum creatinine) was only reported in patients receiving agalsidase alfa (Table 3).

During a global shortage of agalsidase beta in 2009, many patients switched to agalsidase alfa, which allowed for the real-world assessment of differences in treatment response over time. A systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies determined that, in general, there was no change in renal function during the course of this switch. Although one study showed a benefit with agalsidase alfa when assessing cystatin C-based eGFR and creatinine/cystatin C-based eGFR, other studies have reported some cases of worsening renal function after switching to agalsidase alfa. A Latin American study assessing the effects of switching from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa (which was not included in this meta-analysis) also showed no change in mean eGFR over a 24-month follow-up period.

In a subsequent meta-analysis and systematic review of patients who switched from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa, a significant loss of renal function after switching was observed in 4 of the 15 studies; this was not reversed despite agalsidase alfa dose increases. Lyso-GL-3 levels decreased after patients switched back to agalsidase beta, which suggests that there was a dose-dependent effect and/or that agalsidase beta was more advantageous in these patients. In one of the included studies, eGFR improved following the switch back to agalsidase beta. Three studies have demonstrated a continuous decline in eGFR in patients with FD switched from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa; in one of the studies, this decline was attenuated in patients who had switched back to agalsidase beta. Therefore, it has been suggested that, rather than eGFR, plasma lyso-GL-3 levels may be a more sensitive indicator of treatment response after switching back to agalsidase beta.

Taken together, these data highlight the importance of initiating ERT prior to the development of renal disease. Moreover, data on switching to higher doses of agalsidase alfa indicated that loss of renal function was not prevented. As such, long-term post-switch data suggest a benefit with agalsidase beta over agalsidase alfa.

In patients with FD, eGFR generally remains stable over the course of treatment with migalastat, with most studies reporting non-significant eGFR decline (Table 4). To our knowledge, however, two studies have reported a significant eGFR decline with migalastat; in one study, renal function decreased after 1 year of migalastat therapy, and, in some cases, plasma lyso-GL-3 levels increased after switching to migalastat therapy, while, in the other study, eGFR decreased by - 5.0 mL/min/1.73 m2 in females and by - 4.6 mL/min/1.73 m2 in males after 12 months of migalastat treatment. The yearly loss in eGFR was more moderate after 24 months of migalastat treatment (- 2.6 mL/min/1.73 m2/year in females and - 4.4 mL/min/1.73 m2/year in males). A post hoc analysis of a combined phase 3 and extension study reported that renal function was relatively stable regardless of sex, phenotype, or treatment status. Another post hoc analysis of phase 3 studies determined that migalastat-treated patients with amenable GLA variants had fewer clinical events (including renal events) than ERT-treated patients over 18 months. Interestingly, this analysis found that a higher baseline eGFR was a predictor for experiencing a clinical event.

Two studies support the renal benefits of migalastat, with treatment providing a reduction in GL-3 levels in renal endothelial cells. When migalastat was compared with other ERTs in a phase 3 migalastat trial, there was no significant difference between treatment groups in the reduction of renal function over time (Table 4). However, further research is warranted to determine whether the effect of migalastat on renal outcomes is due to migalastat or instead due to a continuation of treatment following 12 months of prior ERT. Real-world data from an analysis of the Fabry Registry emphasize the importance of careful monitoring after switching patients from agalsidase beta to migalastat. This analysis described within-patient clinical outcomes for patients with FD treated with agalsidase beta for >= 1 year as first primary therapy, followed by >= 6 months of migalastat as second primary therapy; the study inclusion cut-off date was 7 April 2023. The assessments of eGFR and plasma GL-3 suggested that disease progression occurred after switching (both for the comparison of before and after switching and in linear mixed models).

As mentioned above, migalastat is only indicated in patients who have an amenable GLA variant. Consequently, while migalastat may have favorable effects on renal function, these benefits do not apply to all patients with FD.
Neurological Involvement in FD

Patients with FD can present with CNS complications, such as cerebral small vessel disease (SVD), characterized by white matter hyperintensities, cerebral microbleeds, and cerebral infarcts. In one study, 45% of patients with FD presented with white matter lesions (WMLs) at their first visit to the clinic, with the likelihood of WMLs significantly increasing with age. Phenotypic differences were reported for both sexes; those with classical FD were significantly more likely to have WMLs than those with non-classical FD, and males were more likely to have WMLs than females. There is a strong correlation between WML severity and the speed of cognitive deterioration, and clinical disease severity in patients with FD. Of the neurological effects, cerebrovascular events are the most common and can be the most clinically disabling affliction, with a poorly understood pathogenesis.

Age is an important factor with regard to the neurological effects of FD. It is a predictor of SVD, with older patients having a higher risk of stroke than younger patients; of note, patients with FD tend to develop SVD at a younger age than the general population. However, in general, the cerebrovascular effects in younger patients with FD is not well studied.
Neurological Effects of Agalsidase Beta

In a study of the effects of agalsidase beta on WML progression, the proportion of patients with stable WML burden was significantly greater among patients receiving ERT than in those receiving placebo (Table 1). Notably, there was a clinically and statistically significant reduction or stabilization of WML load in patients aged <= 50 years up to 33 months after treatment initiation. In addition, this study highlighted the importance of initiating treatment prior to serious organ involvement, with a correlation found between left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and WML burden. Finally, a meta-analysis of seven cohort studies and two randomized controlled trials found that ERT for FD had a beneficial effect on stroke prevention.
Neurological Effects of Agalsidase Alfa

Few studies have investigated the effect agalsidase alfa has on the CNS as a primary aim (Table 2). In a small study investigating CNS involvement following 1 year of agalsidase alfa treatment in four patients who had WMLs at baseline, two patients remained stable and two experienced worsening of WMLs.

Hearing impairment is substantially more prevalent in patients with FD compared with a healthy population of equivalent age. In a study of male patients with FD, there was a significant long-term benefit of agalsidase alfa for high-frequency hearing, although no benefit was observed for low-frequency hearing, while, overall, hearing deteriorated during the first 6 months of treatment. A subsequent retrospective study showed similar findings, with improvements seen in some male patients with FD, although none of the female patients with hearing loss regained any hearing. These findings suggest that agalsidase alfa may improve some of the neurological effects of FD, but more data are needed to provide clarity.
Comparative Effects of Agalsidase Alfa Versus Agalsidase Beta

The head-to-head comparison study of agalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta at the same dose (0.2 mg/kg EOW; i.e., an unlicensed dose of agalsidase beta) by Vedder and colleagues did not assess neurological benefits over time; however, five of the six patients with treatment failure over 24 months had progression of brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (three receiving agalsidase beta and two receiving agalsidase alfa). One patient receiving agalsidase alfa died of cerebral infarction after 20 months of treatment (Table 3).

passages.text: In the systematic review and meta-analysis assessing the switch from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa, only one study investigated neurological effects, with no significant differences observed over the study period. In a comparative systematic review of ERT in seven cohort studies assessing agalsidase beta and five investigating agalsidase alfa, linear regression showed that agalsidase beta was associated with a significantly lower incidence of cerebrovascular complications than agalsidase alfa or no treatment.
Neurological Effects of Migalastat

Despite the expectation that migalastat should cross the blood-brain barrier, to date, there are no studies available investigating its CNS effects, most likely due to the more recent approval of this agent compared with agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta.
Cardiovascular Involvement in FD

According to the Fabry Outcome Survey, cardiac disease is the main cause of death among patients with FD, regardless of whether or not they receive ERT. Cardiac complications may be subtle in children and adolescents with FD, and progressively worsen as the patient ages.
