The green line indicates cumulative penetrance. Reproduced from with permission from Elsevier. No. number, NT-proBNP N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide

A sex-specific difference in cardiovascular complications was observed in a study of 182 patients with FD who underwent cardiovascular MRI. LVH was significantly more prevalent in males than females, the prevalence increased with age in both sexes. A similar pattern of male- and age-prevalence was observed with late gadolinium enhancement (Fig. 2).
Cardiovascular Effects of Agalsidase Beta
Several studies have shown cardiac benefits following agalsidase beta treatment, as well as a stabilizing effect in other studies (Table 1).

Of note, the majority of studies used echocardiography to assess cardiovascular effects, which has inferior precision to cardiac MRI. Two studies used cardiac MRI to evaluate the cardiovascular effects, both of which demonstrated benefits with agalsidase beta. The first of these studies showed significant improvements in cardiovascular measures and an amelioration of clinical cardiological symptoms in all patients receiving agalsidase beta for 2 years. In the second study, agalsidase beta provided significant improvements in peak systolic strain and end-diastolic strain of the posterior wall over 1 year, as determined by color Doppler myocardial imaging, while echocardiography showed a reduction in end-diastolic posterior wall thickness. In addition to these benefits, MRI showed a reduction in myocardial mass. These results indicate that agalsidase beta may improve regional myocardial function and reduce LVH in patients with FD. An early phase 3 trial of agalsidase beta reported clearance of GL-3 in cardiac capillary endothelial cells for most patients after only 6 months of treatment, indicating a positive impact on cardiac tissue. However, previous studies have indicated that capillary endothelium clearance does not necessarily reflect myocyte clearance.

The benefits of agalsidase beta treatment may be dependent on the extent of underlying cardiac disease at the time of treatment initiation (Table 1). In a small study in children who had no cardiac abnormalities at baseline, there were no changes in cardiac parameters after 48 months of agalsidase beta treatment. In another small study, six out of ten pediatric patients developed valvular involvement during the 8-year follow up period (at 6-21 years of age), as measured by echocardiography; however, none had subjective symptoms. Two patients, one with mild LVH at baseline and one with mild tricuspid valve insufficiency, had normal echocardiography findings after 1 year of receiving agalsidase beta. No electrocardiography abnormalities were reported during the study.

In a detailed investigation of the cardiac effects of agalsidase beta, a significant proportion of patients with FD without signs or symptoms of cardiac involvement at baseline had more subtle indications of reduced cardiac health compared with healthy controls. In this study, agalsidase beta significantly improved orthostatic regulation and baroreflex sensitivity, with improvements in heart rate, blood pressure and sympathetic activation over 18 or 23 months.

A long-term study showed that cardiac hypertrophy progressed during the pre-treatment period, as assessed by left ventricular posterior wall thickness (LVPWT) and interventricular septal thickness (IVST), but appeared to stabilize after agalsidase beta treatment. In another long-term study of patients treated for > 10 years with agalsidase beta, LVPWT and IVST remained within normal ranges in patients aged < 40 years (with no LVH at baseline). However, patients aged > 40 years (with LVH at baseline), had a significant increase in LVH despite receiving agalsidase beta. Of note, another study demonstrated a link between the effects of agalsidase beta on cardiac function and renal function. Although a non-significant reduction in posterior wall thickness (PWT) was observed overall, the reduction in PWT was found to be significant among patients with preserved renal function. This highlights the importance of monitoring the effects of treatment on all major organ systems affected by FD.

These studies demonstrate that agalsidase beta may provide cardiovascular benefits in patients with FD, although the extent of cardiac disease, which tends to progress with increasing age, may affect the degree of measurable treatment effectiveness.
Cardiovascular Effects of Agalsidase Alfa
Several studies investigating agalsidase alfa therapy in patients with FD have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits, and a stabilizing effect (Table 2).

All studies investigating agalsidase alfa used either echocardiology or cardiac MRI to measure cardiac parameters; in cases where echocardiology alone was used, the accuracy of the results may be somewhat limited. Compared with placebo, 6 months' agalsidase alfa treatment was associated with a non-significant reduction (P = 0.47) in myocardial GL-3 levels, with a significant reduction of left ventricular mass (LVM) only in the first 6 months of treatment, followed by no change over 2 years. Of note, quantification of myocardial GL-3 was performed by high-performance liquid chromatography using whole myocardial samples, thus not providing any data on effective myocyte clearance, with the measured reduction likely sustained by endothelial cell clearance.

A few long-term studies have examined differences in treatment response based on sex and underlying disease state; however, the results were contradictory (Table 2). A retrospective study showed that the LVM index (LVMI) remained relatively stable with agalsidase alfa over 10 years, but patients who had LVH at baseline had a slight increase in LVMI, which was observed in both male and female patients. Similarly, in another retrospective study, LVMI significantly improved with 1 year of treatment, although the only significant improvement observed after 10 years was in males with a baseline LVMI of >= 50 g/m2.7. Improvements in other cardiac structural parameters were also observed in male patients, including a significant reduction in mean wall thickness. Most changes in cardiac functional parameters during agalsidase alfa treatment were similar between the sexes. In contrast, in a retrospective study, only female patients with baseline LVH experienced a significant decrease in LVMI after 4 years of agalsidase alfa treatment. Likewise, in a female-only study with baseline LVH in 69% of patients, agalsidase alfa was associated with a significant decrease in LVM, and many patients with New York Heart Association class II-III heart failure showed improvement over 4 years.

Only one study has examined the effects of agalsidase alfa in pediatric patients with FD. The majority of patients had no change in cardiac function over 2 years, although 7 of 22 patients developed T-wave abnormalities and 3 developed LVH.

These findings suggest that agalsidase alfa may improve cardiac parameters, although further research is required to determine possible long-term clinical cardiovascular benefits or whether there are sex-specific differences in treatment response.
Comparative Effects of Agalsidase Beta Versus Agalsidase Alfa

The majority of studies comparing the cardiovascular effects of agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta report a switch from one agent to another (Table 3). In the systematic review and meta-analysis of the agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa switch, two studies reported cardiac improvements post-switch to agalsidase alfa, and one study reported worsening of IVST. Another study in this review demonstrated that, although left ventricular ejection fraction was unchanged in ERT-naive patients who initiated agalsidase beta, and remained unchanged post-switch to agalsidase alfa, there were significant decreases in LVMI and LV wall thickness that were maintained post-switch to agalsidase alfa. Another study of Japanese patients reported a significant improvement in LVMI from baseline (where patients had been receiving agalsidase beta) to 12 months post-switch to agalsidase alfa. In another switching study (which was not included in the meta-analysis), there was no change in LVMI, IVS, or LVPWT after switching from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa. A subsequent meta-analysis and systematic review of switching ERTs showed that cardiac parameters remained generally stable post-switch to agalsidase alfa, with one patient across the studies reporting a significant worsening of LVH.

A comparative systematic review that included four studies of agalsidase alfa and three of agalsidase beta versus untreated patients, found that agalsidase beta was associated with significantly fewer cardiovascular complications than untreated patients. However, no significant differences in cardiovascular events were seen between agalsidase alfa and agalsidase beta or no ERT.

In a 1-year retrospective study of both agalsidase beta and agalsidase alfa by Arends and colleagues in 2018, combined treatment data showed a decrease in LVMI only in patients who had baseline LVH, irrespective of treatment received; however, a higher proportion of patients treated with agalsidase beta had a LVMI decrease when adjusted for baseline levels. Although all of these studies demonstrated cardiovascular benefits with ERT (Table 3), the study suggests that agalsidase beta may provide better cardiac outcomes than agalsidase alfa. More head-to-head comparative studies of ERTs in patients with FD are warranted.

In the head-to-head ERT study of agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg EOW (i.e., an unlicensed dose of agalsidase beta) by Vedder and colleagues, no LVM reduction was observed with either treatment after 12 or 24 months of follow-up. Treatment failure due to atrial fibrillation (i.e. cardiac disease progression) occurred in three patients: one male patient and one female patient after 42 and 36 months of agalsidase beta treatment, respectively, and in one male patient treated with agalsidase alfa for 30 months.

Sex-specific differences in cardiovascular outcomes have been reported with the ERTs in patients with FD. A study that used cardiac MRI to assess the impact of ERT on cardiovascular parameters assessed 100 patients (37 on agalsidase alfa, 13 on agalsidase beta, and 50 untreated) over a median of 37 months. There were no sex-specific differences observed in cardiac parameters (including ischemic heart disease or hypertension); however, males had more baseline cardiac involvement than females and tended to have higher rates of disease progression, despite the use of an ERT. These data support the cardiovascular benefits of ERTs and reinforce the need for early treatment initiation.
Cardiovascular Effects of Migalastat

Multiple studies have demonstrated the cardiovascular benefits of migalastat, with significant reductions in LVMI seen with echocardiographic evaluations over the course of treatment; in all these studies, the effect of migalastat on LVMI was evaluated by echocardiography not by MRI (Table 4). Of note, the benefits of migalastat do not appear to be sex-specific, with significant LVMI reductions observed in both male and female patients with FD. Importantly, within many studies, a significant LVMI reduction was observed in patients with baseline LVH.

Significant improvements in LVMI from baseline were observed in a study of male patients with FD after switching from agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta to migalastat, although patients with abnormal cardiac parameters had no improvement with either treatment. In a comparative trial, migalastat treatment for 18 months led to a small, but statistically significant, reduction in LVMI; in contrast, the reduction in LVMI with agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta did not reach statistical significance. This evidence suggests that migalastat ameliorates selected cardiac parameters.

Although these data provide evidence for the cardiovascular benefits of migalastat, these studies all measured cardiac parameters using echocardiography. However, a more recent study, which used cardiac MRI, showed stabilization of LVM and an increase in T1 over 18 months of treatment with migalastat in a small group of treatment-naive patients with baseline cardiac involvement. Notably, the majority of patients (81.3%) had a late-onset phenotype of FD. At 18 months' follow-up, a tendency to increasing troponin T values in the entire study population was noted, from a baseline median of 8.0 (range 4.0-21.0) ng/L to 14.5 (3.5-26.0) ng/L, which was above the normal value and approaching statistical significance (P = 0.06).
Other Disease Manifestations and Quality of Life

While the abovementioned organ systems are the primary focus of FD treatment to prevent disease progression and preserve life, patients also experience other disease manifestations, such as diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain, that affect their QoL. The pathophysiological mechanisms of gastrointestinal complications in FD are still not clear, with the symptomatology presenting similarly to diarrhea-predominant inflammatory bowel syndrome. Pain, particularly neuropathic pain, is often one of the earliest symptoms of FD in most patients and a significant contributor to reduced QoL. Therefore, it is important to determine the impact of available treatments on these factors.
Effects of Agalsidase Beta

A few studies have shown the benefits of agalsidase beta on the gastrointestinal system (Table 1). Agalsidase beta was associated with marked improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms in a prospective study of 25 patients with FD. In another study, patients with severe gastrointestinal symptoms had a marked improvement after 8 months of agalsidase beta treatment. This finding was supported by data from the Fabry Registry, in which male patients with classic or later-onset FD had a general reduction in gastrointestinal symptoms with agalsidase beta. At treatment initiation, a higher proportion of patients with the classical phenotype had abdominal pain and diarrhea than those with the later-onset phenotype; following treatment, significant reductions in these symptoms were only observed in patients with the classical phenotype. Data from the Fabry Registry on female patients receiving agalsidase beta showed an improvement in the proportion of patients with abdominal pain (from 45 to 31%) and diarrhea (from 39 to 27%) over a mean follow-up of 5.7 years.

Across a few studies, patients reported improvements in pain and QoL with agalsidase beta (Table 1). A study of ten children with FD found variation in the symptomatology over 8 years of treatment with agalsidase beta, with all patients reporting having more energy and nine engaging in more physical activity. Five patients had improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms, and most of those with headaches at baseline reported improvements. Another pediatric study reported encouraging results with regard to improvements in QoL, including a significant increase in the number of school days. Another Fabry Registry study reported significant improvements with agalsidase beta across all Short-Form 36 (SF-36) Health Survey physical and mental component summary scores among male patients. There is evidence to support the benefits of agalsidase beta on reducing gastrointestinal and pain symptoms and improving patient QoL.
Effects of Agalsidase Alfa

Although data relating to the effects of agalsidase alfa on pain and QoL are limited, this ERT also appears to provide some benefits. The Fabry Outcome Survey study reported significant improvements in the EuroQoL-Five Dimensions utility score and Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) score among 304 patients receiving agalsidase alfa (Table 2). Similarly, a study of female patients with FD reported a significant reduction in the 'worst pain' BPI score with 1 year of agalsidase alfa treatment. A 4-year Fabry Outcome Survey study of agalsidase alfa treatment in female versus male patients with FD reported no change in the prevalence of pain attacks or abdominal pain in females; however, in comparison to symptoms at baseline, there was a reduction in diarrhea (from 32 to 26%) and body pain (from 28 to 21%). For males, there was almost no change in abdominal pain or diarrhea from baseline, and a slight increase in body pain, while pain attacks were reduced (from 73 to 68%).

In one study of 342 patients with FD, which investigated the effects of agalsidase alfa on gastrointestinal symptoms and QoL, there was a reduction in the proportion of patients with gastrointestinal symptoms after 24 months' treatment. Children and male patients had significant symptomatic improvements during treatment, with no children experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms after treatment initiation.
These findings indicate that further investigations into sex-specific differences underlying the effects of agalsidase alfa on pain and QoL are warranted.
Comparative Effects of Agalsidase Beta Versus Agalsidase Alfa

As discussed above, only one study has directly compared agalsidase beta and agalsidase alfa. Within this head-to-head study, there was no significant reduction in BPI score with either ERT after 12 or 24 months of treatment at the same 0.2-mg/kg EOW dose (i.e., an unlicensed dose of agalsidase beta). In the systematic review and meta-analysis of the switch from agalsidase beta to agalsidase alfa, three studies investigating pain showed no difference in severity post-switch, whereas one study reported fewer pain attacks; however, the latter study also reported worsening of gastrointestinal symptoms post-switch. Three studies investigated changes in QoL, with no changes observed post-switch. The other switching study reported that SF-36 physical functioning and BPI scores had improved following the switch to agalsidase alfa.

The most recent meta-analysis and systematic review of switching found that most symptoms were stable post-switch; however, two studies reported a worsening of Mainz Severity Score Index (MSSI) in patients who switched to agalsidase alfa and in those who switched back to agalsidase beta. Interestingly, the recent studies in this meta-analysis showed an increase in pain symptoms in patients on agalsidase alfa that improved after switching back to agalsidase beta.

Overall, there are mixed results regarding the potential benefits of one agalsidase over the other; however, more recent long-term follow-up data showing improvements in pain after the switch back to agalsidase beta warrants further investigation.
Effects of Migalastat

In the phase 3 FACETS study, 6 months of treatment with migalastat was associated with significant reductions in diarrhea compared with placebo (Table 4), as well as a small improvement in the Gastrointestinal Symptoms Rating Scale subscale score. Although no major improvements were seen in a 2-year observational study during migalastat treatment, pain, MSSI, and Depression and Somatic Symptoms Scale scores remained stable (Table 4).

When compared with ERTs, one study reported migalastat was associated with similar SF-36 and BPI scores; in a separate study, BPI scores only improved with ERT and remained stable with migalastat. These data suggest that migalastat has a beneficial effect on improving diarrhea in patients with FD and may reduce pain symptoms and prevent the deterioration of QoL.
Preliminary Data on the Effects of Pegunigalsidase Alfa in FD

Pegunigalsidase alfa has been recently approved for the treatment of FD in Europe and the US. Two phase 3 clinical trials (BRIDGE and BALANCE) have been published to date; data from a third phase 3 clinical trial (BRIGHT) are currently available as a congress abstract and in a European Medicines Agency Assessment Report (EMA EPAR). The first clinical study (BRIDGE) evaluated the open-label use of pegunigalsidase alfa (1 mg/kg every 2 weeks) in adults with FD who had previously received agalsidase alfa in a 3-month dose-ranging study, followed by a 9-month extension. Switching to pegunigalsidase alfa was well tolerated and provided additional clinical benefit, particularly with respect to the kidney function trajectory and the FD biomarker plasma lyso-globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in most patients. The BALANCE study was conducted in adults with FD and an annualized eGFR slope of lower than - 2 mL/min/1.73 m2/year and who had been treated with agalsidase beta for >= 1 year, to assess the non-inferiority of pegunigalsidase alfa versus agalsidase beta. Patients were randomly assigned 2:1 to receive pegunigalsidase alfa 1 mg/kg or agalsidase beta every 2 weeks for 2 years. Although pegunigalsidase alfa was non-inferior to agalsidase beta after 24 months of treatment for annualized eGFR slope (final analysis), non-inferiority could not be demonstrated at the 12-month interim analysis (results available in the EMA EPAR). Indeed, interim analysis results indicated a difference in annualized eGFR slope in favor of agalsidase beta [difference of - 0.749 mL/min/1.73 m2, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.03-1.51]. The open-label BRIGHT study investigated an alternative dosing regimen for pegunigalsidase alfa, of 2 mg/kg once every 4 weeks, in patients who had switched from either agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta. Study results were inconclusive, and, indeed, 2 mg/kg once every 4 weeks is not an approved dose of pegunigalsidase alfa.
Unmet Clinical Needs in Patients with FD

As FD is highly heterogenous, it can be challenging to diagnose and manage. The Fabry Registry data showed that patients with FD tend to experience their first symptoms at a young age; however, ERT tends to only be initiated decades later. Bridging the gap between symptom onset and diagnosis remains a critical clinical need. Although guidelines addressing the management of FD are available, they are complex and divided by sex and/or clinical phenotype. This may be due (in part) to the influence of sex and clinical phenotype on the clinical complexity of FD.

In a study by El Sayed and colleagues, in which 213 patients with FD (median age 50 years) were evaluated from birth to last visit, the rate of major cardiovascular events (including death, cardiovascular death, heart failure hospitalization, sustained ventricular arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, conduction abnormality, and atrial fibrillation) was 11.0 per 1000 patient-years (95% CI 6.6-17.3) in males with classical FD, 4.4 per 1000 patient-years (95% CI 2.5-7.1) in females with classical FD and 5.9 per 1000 patient-years (95% CI 2.6-11.6) in males with non-classical FD. None of the females with non-classical FD had major cardiovascular events. Sex and phenotype significantly influenced the risk of major cardiovascular events, indicating the need for patient-specific follow-up and treatment.

Recommendations from an international panel of FD specialists specify that males with classical FD should receive treatment regardless of symptoms, whereas females with classical FD should only receive treatment following the appearance of major organ injury. Unfortunately, while female patients are less adversely affected by FD, they can experience varied symptomatology and there is some evidence that they are undertreated. In one study, female patients were treated with ERTs substantially less frequently than males (34% vs. 82%, respectively), and some untreated female patients had major organ involvement, including LVH.

Despite the benefits of available treatment options, none can substantially reverse the major organ damage caused by FD progression. Of these treatments, ERT does not provide dramatic improvements in outcomes for all organ systems. This is probably due to the pathophysiological pathway at the origin of the disease where different mechanisms (storage, inflammation, apoptosis, etc.) lead to chronic and non-reversible tissue damage, such as sclerosis and fibrosis. To date, no therapeutic options have offered substantial amelioration of organ dysfunction; instead, they provide various grades of stabilization in progressive end-organ damage and the related functioning slope.

passages.text: Various studies have shown correlations between major organ systems and disease progression. While children and adolescents may not show obvious signs of cardiac complications, careful screening has highlighted subtle abnormalities that are understood to be LVH precursors. Therefore, all three treatments should be initiated prior to disease progression and the development of irreversible pathological organs changes, which may help to address the abovementioned unmet clinical needs.
An Optimal and Practical Therapeutic Approach: Authors' Perspective

The developments in FD treatment over the past 20 years has significantly changed the natural history of the disease and has improved patient survival, morbidity, and QoL. However, in some cases, the introduction of FD therapy is unable to reverse symptoms or arrest/slow disease progression. There can be several reasons for therapeutical failure, including a delayed diagnosis, delayed treatment initiation, or variable drug efficacy. Alternatively, in some cases, therapy is administered in the presence of polymorphisms or benign mutations (e.g., the D313Y variant), diverting resources from patients who may be severely affected. In these cases, eventual symptoms (often neurological, and similar to those documented in FD), are not due to the disease but are only concomitant and cannot be resolved by/cannot benefit from FD therapies.

Since FD is a progressive disease that can lead to organ failure, an optimal therapeutic approach relies on more than just an early diagnosis. Minimizing the time between the onset of symptoms and diagnosis, as well as the time between diagnosis and initiation of treatment, is likely to improve the effect of therapy on signs and symptoms. However, an early diagnosis should not take precedence over the correct diagnosis. Indeed, before the choice of a specific treatment is made, it is crucial to achieve the correct FD diagnosis. The increasing number of new variants and VUS can make it difficult to determine the real pathogenic role of the variant, which in turn makes it challenging to accurately determine when to start therapy or which drug to administer to a specific patient.

The definition of a real phenotype should start from a familial evaluation of disease burden, also considering possible intrafamilial variability. Thereafter, a complete patient investigation (clinical, biochemical, and histopathological examination) is required to confirm or exclude the pathogenic role of a GLA variant. At present, it is generally thought that elevated levels of lyso-GL-3 and the ultrastructural presence of zebra-bodies in tissue biopsies are the most relevant elements to distinguish pathogenic variants from benign variants, especially if they are new or a VUS. Therefore, a multidisciplinary approach that can aid in making the correct diagnosis is recommended before the initiation of a particular therapy. Geneticists and clinicians should seek advice/collaboration with other physicians involved in the diagnosis and management of FD.

Once the correct phenotype and disease burden has been established, it is necessary to identify the therapeutic goals of each patient. Improvement of signs/symptoms such as pain and albuminuria is possible if treatment starts very early in childhood or adolescence. However, if diagnosis is delayed and treatment begins in adulthood, in the presence of proteinuria, or initial LVH, therapeutic goals should be adjusted to aim for at least the stabilization of signs and symptoms and the reduction of disease progression. Finally, in the advanced phases of the disease, the presence of chronic renal failure or advanced cardiac involvement may limit the achievement of therapeutic goals.

The choice of the best treatment strategy should not be based only on therapeutic goals but also on other factors. Genotype, phenotype, age of onset, onset symptom, and disease burden are the main factors that a multidisciplinary team should consider in the choice of treatment strategy. Personalizing or individualizing the choice of treatment should be based on the decision-making of an expert team and physicians should not be influenced entirely by the desires of the patient. For example, patients may prefer oral therapy to intravenous therapy, but there may be no clinical indication towards this treatment. Similarly, a home treatment setting may not always represent the best choice for a patient who shows limited treatment compliance.

In relation to the progression of nephropathy in patients with FD, a recent expert opinion paper has pointed out the role of an elevated eGFR slope as a possible factor that may be able to modify and adjust the therapeutic strategy in patients with FD. Based on data of the effects of ERTs on eGFR decline and of the evidence supporting the role of eGFR slopes as a surrogate endpoint for CKD progression, the authors suggest that a treatment should be deemed effective when the eGFR decline is < 1 mL/min/1.73 m2/year and not effective when eGFR loss remains >= 3 mL/min/1.73 m2/year in males or >= 2.5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year in females (Fig. 3). This leads to practical clinical recommendations and guidance for patients with FD, and suggests that a change in treatment may be appropriate if individualized therapeutic goals are not achieved.

There is limited consensus on the timing of treatment initiation in FD. Initiating treatment at diagnosis in male children with classic severe variants and at diagnosis in adult male patients is less controversial, but there is more difficulty around the decision of treatment initiation in females. In our opinion, adult females with a classic variant who are symptomatic for at least one sign or have symptoms of organ involvement should initiate treatment very soon after the diagnosis. Young females with late-onset variants and a benign course of disease in family members do not require immediate initiation, but should be monitored closely until the onset of signs or symptoms. In all cases, concomitant adjunctive treatment should be considered if specific therapies do not completely remove signs or symptoms (such as pain or proteinuria).

If therapeutic goals are not achieved, then a change in treatment should be considered to arrest disease progression. Several reports have documented a positive effect on disease progression when using an increased dose of infused agalsidase. Furthermore, the switch from agalsidase alfa to agalsidase beta has been shown to attenuate the steepness of eGFR slope decline in patients with normal or mild chronic renal failure.
The above treatment and strategy considerations aim to improve the management of patients in clinical practice to provide better outcomes and an improved QoL.
Conclusions

FD is a debilitating disease that negatively impacts the renal, neurological, and cardiovascular systems, in addition to QoL. Patients often present with substantial, irreversible organ damage, and management of this heterogenous population is challenging. While all four available treatment options offer benefits, migalastat is only appropriate for patients with amenable GLA variants. Agalsidase beta shows beneficial effects across the renal, neurological, and cardiovascular systems, as well as compelling QoL improvements, and may help prevent renal disease progression. Moreover, agalsidase beta has demonstrated a stabilizing effect in patients previously treated with agalsidase alfa. Limited data are available on the efficacy of pegunigalsidase alfa at present. Mounting evidence suggests that relative disease progression often occurs across organ systems and that subtle pathological changes may develop without overt signs or symptoms, even in pediatric patients. This suggests that treatment effectiveness depends on early treatment initiation and the dose delivered to maximize benefits, improve QoL, and prolong life.

passages.text: Rediscovering the chemistry of the Cunninghamella species: potential fungi for metabolites and enzymes of biological, industrial, and environmental values

Endophytic fungi have a strong affinity for producing the same or comparable compounds to those produced by their hosts. Herein, genetic diversity and environmental adaptation of the Cunninghamella species were briefly investigated. The genetic flexibility in Cunninghamella represents an evolutionary mechanism that allows them to respond effectively to environmental changes. The current review paid much attention toward the phytochemical screening of Cunninghamella sp., revealing the presence of alkaloids, unsaturated sterols, fatty acids, polyphenols, and quinones. The intensive investigations clarified that Cunninghamella sp. are distinguished in producing several numbers of fatty acids, in particular polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), in large quantities compared to other metabolites. The study demonstrated the effective role of Cunninghamella sp. in forming several bioactive metabolites owing to cytochrome P450 (CYP) that confirm significant value of such species for potential media biotransformation. The comparative investigations revealed that the isolation of flavonoids is yet to be reported, while the number of elucidated alkaloids and steroids is still limited. In contrast, successful results in the biotransformation of these metabolites were verified and showed a high affinity to convert simple substances to more valuable agents by Cunninghamella. The biomedical applications of naturally occurring compounds isolated from Cunninghamella were well documented; these included their antimicrobial, anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, anti-Alzheimer, and antiaging properties. The antimicrobial activity was mostly attributed to the fatty acid contents in Cunninghamella sp. Moreover, tremendous attention was paid towards the agricultural and industrial usage of chitosan as it is one of the most crucial metabolites involved in wide applications. Chitosan is involved in food preservation for extending life storage period and utilized as biofertilizer, which enhances bacterial disease resistance. In addition, Cunninghamella is considered an important enzyme reservoir. Various Cunninghamella sp. produce several important enzymes, such as lignin peroxidase, catalase, cellulase, xylanase, laccase, and CYPs, that can be used for remediation, fertilization, preservation and medicinal purposes. Hence, further in-depth investigations are highly recommended to explore new insights into this potential reservoir of a wide spectrum of chemicals for industrial, medicinal, agricultural, and environmental applications.
Cunninghamella fungi have its unique chemistry that provide potential metabolites applicable for biological, industrial, and environmental fields.
Introduction

Endophytic fungi are microorganisms that reside within the tissues of the host plant without exhibiting any outward signs of illness. Several novel endophytic fungi have been recently isolated from different plant species and implemented for several medical and industrial purposes. Endophytes from plants are reported to be a source of several new lead compounds with potential uses in different fields, such as medicine, agriculture, environment, and industry. Endophytic fungi can produce metabolites like those of their host plants, such as flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, coumarins, steroids, and lignans. Previously isolated fungal metabolites have verified that the diversity in biological activities encompasses antioxidant, anticancer, antimicrobial, anti-respiratory syncytial, antiproliferative and antibacterial functions.. For instance, a myriad of biologically active components, including terpenoids, alkaloids and flavonoids, were isolated from the Phyllosticta sp. fungus, which showed potent antioxidant activity. In addition, a recent phytochemical study successfully utilized the endophytic fungi Coniolariella hispanica, Penicillium canescens, Paraphoma radicina and P. murcianum as precursors for producing cryptotanshinone as a terpene compound that considered the principal metabolite like the host Salvia abrotanoides plant. An additional distinctive bioactive agent was identified with 3-hydroxy-4-(hydroxy(4-hydroxyphenyl) methyl) dihydrofuran-2-on from Fusarium verticillioides, proving its antibacterial activity. Mellein and beta-retinaldehyde were also isolated from the endophytic fungus Botryosphaeria fabicerciana, of which its potential efficacy as antioxidant and antimicrobial was revealed. Beside its effective role in biological activity, endophytic fungi also enhanced plant growth and development via the secretion of different enzymes involved in the biotechnological and industrial sectors.

Taking into consideration the potential attention paid towards endophytic fungi, Mucorales is the largest order. This order belongs to the phylum Zygomycota, subphylum Mucoromycotina that comprises 15 families, 57 genera and 334 species.Cunninghamella (family Cunninghamellaceae) was the most predominated genus belonging to Mucorales order and is one of the most potential fungi which has been investigated deeply.Cunninghamella was first established by Matruchot in 1903 upon collection of C. africana in the French Sudan, which would later be known as C. echinulata.Cunninghamella sp. has a strong ability to produce sporophores with uni-spored sporangia that are pedicellate on the vesicle surface and coated in spines. The sporophores have an uneven, pseudo-vertical, or verticillate branching shape. Furthermore, the majority of Cunninghamella sp. are saprobes, which are frequently founded in soil, stored grains, and other organic substrates. On the other hand, to identify additional species belonging to Cunninghamella, physical properties can be used, such as the colony color, texture, pattern of sporophore branching, vesicle form and size, sporangia shape and size, and the presence or absence, and length of spines in the sporangia. Based on the phylogenetic analyses and morphological characters, there are about 17 species of Cunninghamella that have been identified. In immunocompromised patients, such as those who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplants or hematological malignancies, some Cunninghamella sp. such as C. bertholletiae,C. blakesleeana,C. echinulata,C. elegans and C. arunalokei, can cause mucormycosis, an angioinvasive illness that primarily manifests as pulmonary and disseminated infections. Different Cunninghamella sp. can produce a variety of secondary metabolites with promising medical and industrial values. Intensive and recent investigations have triggered attention toward the successful utilization of the Cunninghamella species in drug fabrication, owing to the presence of CYP-450 monooxygenase systems that are analogous to those in mammals. In addition, Cunninghamella is regarded as a major source of a wide range of enzymes that can be employed in industry, bioremediation, and biotechnological features, including the biotransformation of various pharmaceutically significant substances like steroids and terpenoids, because it could convert the substrate into highly active compounds.

The current review aims to highlight and extend the potential of the genus Cunninghamella in providing different classes of bioactive secondary metabolites. Interestingly, there is still limitation for direct isolation of lead compounds from Cunninghamella sp. However, most of the intensive investigations have paid more attention to the biotransformation process. Cunninghamella sp. has a strong capacity to use fewer effective compounds as the initial precursors, and convert them into structurally valuable molecules that are widely applied in drugs. This is attributed to the significant genes and enzymes included in Cunninghamella sp. that play an important role in biotransformation, and could be involved in industrial and biotechnological applications. In this review, a broad range of studies have been demonstrated for gaining comprehensive information about Cunninghamella.
Genetic diversity and functional capabilities of the Cunninghamella species

The genus Cunninghamella comprises several key species, including C. elegans, C. bertholletiae, and C. echinulata. These fungi exhibit significant genetic diversity, which influences their biochemical functions and potential applications in various fields.

The CYP-450 genes are essential to the metabolic capabilities of Cunninghamella sp. For instance, the CYP5208A3 gene in C. elegans plays a crucial role in metabolizing a wide variety of chemical compounds. This gene contains coding regions that determine the protein's sequence, as well as regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers, which control gene expression in response to environmental stimuli. The interaction between gene expression and other metabolic pathways enhances the enzyme's ability to chemical processing, demonstrating the organism's adaptability and potential applications, such as pollutant treatment and the development of new chemicals. Environmental adaptation is crucial for the survival and persistence of Cunninghamella sp. in diverse environments. These fungi possess a unique ability to adapt to various environmental conditions, such as temperature, humidity levels, and the presence of pollutants due to their genetic diversity, particularly CYP genes. This genetic diversity enables the fungi to process a wide range of chemical compounds, making them resilient and capable of adapting to environmental changes. For example, exposure to toxic compounds can trigger an increase in the expression of specific CYP genes, enhancing the fungi's ability to neutralize these compounds. The genetic adaptation can directly impact the survival of fungi in polluted or changing environments. Previous investigations suggested that these fungi possess advanced genetic modification capabilities, enhancing them to develop immediate and long-term responses against environmental changes. Studies revealed significant variation in the number of CYP genes amongst different Cunninghamella sp.; for example, C. bertholletiae possess 69 CYP genes, whereas C. elegans have only 32. The variation in gene numbers suggested a greater biochemical transformation capacity in Cunninghamella, influencing its ability to adapt to various chemical environments. Strains with extensive CYP gene families, like those found in C. bertholletiae, can efficiently degrade complex pollutants, thereby supporting their use in biotechnological and environmental contexts. This adaptability highlights the importance of Cunninghamella sp. in addressing pollution and chemical processing challenges.

Cunninghamella sp. exhibit a remarkable ability to adapt to environmental conditions. This adaptability is attributed to the fungi's ability to modulate gene expression in response to environmental conditions. For instance, certain strains of Cunninghamella can modify their genetic makeup to develop resistance against chemical pollutants or environmental changes, giving them a competitive advantage in complex environments. Their ability to produce enzymes that can degrade environmental pollutants or transform industrial chemicals into less harmful substances is particularly notable. For example, C. elegans has been studied for its role in the biotransformation of pharmaceuticals, which highlights its potential in developing environmentally friendly waste treatment processes.
Previously isolated metabolites from Cunninghamella species

Cunninghamella sp. are a valuable source for a plethora of naturally occurring compounds with promising efficiency in biological, industrial, agricultural, and environmental applications. Relevant and recent studies have described the isolation of different secondary metabolites like fatty acids, sterols, phenolic acids, quinones, polysaccharides and nitrogenous compounds from Cunninghamella sp. It is worth mentioning that few compounds have been isolated from Cunninghamella sp., compared to the high numbers of biotransformed metabolites, as presented in Table 1. Cunninghamella has a strong ability to metabolize numerous chemical agents in regio- and stereo-selective strategies, according to the phase I (oxidative) and phase II (conjugative) biotransformation mechanisms. Concurrently, Cunninghamella is considered as one of the significant and distinguished biotechnological techniques regarding biotransformation.

Flavonoids

The bioactive flavonoids represent the most crucial phytochemicals isolated from plants, fungi and other natural sources, revealing a wide range of biological benefits for the human body. The complex structures of flavonoids make their extraction from plants difficult, and there are additional problems associated with the chemical synthesis due to the utilization of several toxic solvents. Microbial production is considered a preferable method for the isolation of these metabolites for industrial applications, as it is a more economical, sustainable and eco-friendly approach. However, with the advances in isolation techniques, microbial production is still limited on a laboratory scale. Furthermore, its enhancement and large-scale fabrication remain a great challenge. Interestingly, despite their potential activity and low toxicity, none of these compounds have yet been isolated directly from Cunninghamella sp., as introduced in Fig. 1. Clearly, based on the literature review, most reported studies have discussed the vital role of Cunninghamella in the successful biotransformation of less effective compounds used as the substrate and converted them into more valuable flavonoids and flavonoid derivatives to maximize their impact in drug discovery (Table 1).

Compared to the isolated flavonoids, several numbers of bio-transformed flavonoids have been facilely produced by Cunninghamella. Noticeably, the basic reactions associated with microbial biotransformation included glycosylation/deglycosylation, carbonyl reduction, hydroxylation/dehydroxylation, O-methylation/O-demethylation, cyclization, hydrogenation/dehydrogenation, sulfation and C ring cleavage of the benzo-gamma-pyrone system.Aspergillus, Penicillium and Cunninghamella sp. are the most prevalent genera in flavonoid biotransformation, and they are distinguished in their ability to perform nearly the entire reactions with significant yields. For instance, C. blakesleeana has been incorporated in the biotransformation of the principal flavonoid glycoside shown in Fig. 2, and is isolated from the herb epimedii for producing a number of rare flavonoids with excellent yield (<95%).Cunninghamella boosts the potential selectivity of C-7 hydrolysis to form a number of unexpected flavonoid glycosides, including icariside II (95.1%), 2-O-rhamnosylikarisoside II (97.7%), epimedoside b (93.7%), baohuoside VII (95.8%) and sagittatoside B (96.4%), as presented in Fig. 2.C. blakesleeana was also utilized in the biotransformation of norkurarinone to kurarinone, 4'',5'' dihydroxynorkurarinone, 7-methoxyl-norkurarinone, 6''-hydroxyl-2'-methoxyl-norkurarinone-7-O-beta-d-glucoside, 6''-hydroxylnorkurarinone-4'-O-beta-d-glucoside, 4'',5''-dihydroxykurarinone and 7-methoxyl-4'',5''-dihydroxynorkurarinone, as shown in Fig. 3. Furthermore, kurarinone was biotransferred to afford flavonoid derivatives using C. echinulata via hydroxylation, dihydroxylation on the C4'' = C5'', O-methylation and glycosylation reactions (Fig. 3) (Table 1).
Bio-transformation of flavonoids to rare flavonoid glycosides by Cunninghamella blakesleeana via hydrolysis reaction.
Biotransformation reaction of norkurarinone by Cunninghamella blakesleeana and C. echinulata.

Another study has introduced the efficient metabolized coumarin into 3,4-dihydrocoumarin, umbelliferone and trans-cinnamic acid using C. elegans NRRL 1392 and dicoumarol, which was transformed into 4-hydroxycoumarin. The produced compounds were characterized by different spectroscopic techniques (e.g., NMR, mass spectrometry) and showed cytotoxic activity (Table 1). In addition, microbial biotransformation of the major flavolignan founded in milk thistle, silybin, by C. blakesleeana resulted in isolation of 2,3-dehydrosilybin 7-sulfate and silybin 7-sulfate, as shown in Fig. 4. A sulfation reaction was induced on C-7 of silybin, which potentially reduced the DPPH free radical scavenging activity. Meanwhile, dehydrogenation at C2 = C3 produced 2,3-dehydrosilybin 7-sulfate, which significantly enhanced the antioxidant activity.
Sulfation and dehydrogenation of the flavonolignan, silybin, by Cunninghamella sp.
As a result, it was clearly observed that Cunninghamella sp. is distinguished for producing diverse and rare flavonoids via the biotransformation process, in comparison to the isolated metabolites.
Alkaloids

A number of recent studies have focused on the isolation of newly discovered alkaloids from plants. However, very few of these molecules have been isolated from Cunninghamella sp. For instance, Inoue et al. discussed the isolation of a new tricyclic alkaloid named ICM020 from Cunninghamella sp. F-1490. The structure of this compound was determined to be (3S, 10aR)-3,4a-dihydroxy-2,3,4,4a-tetrahydro-2H-pyrano[3,2-b]benzo[e]morpholine-9-carboxylic acid using various spectroscopic techniques. This compound was found to have osteoclastogenic inhibitory activity. Using the parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP) test method and tartrate-restricted acid phosphatase (TRAP)-positive multinucleated cells formation assay method, a significant inhibitory impact was demonstrated against the development of osteoclasts in mouse bone marrow cells with an IC50 value of 0.78 mug mL-1. Furthermore, this compound showed weak cytotoxicity against bone marrow cell lines using the trypan blue exclusion assay, which suggested that its cytotoxicity was not a factor in the prevention of osteoclastogenesis. Some nucleosides and nucleotides were also reported from Cunninghamella sp., such as adenosine, uridine and uracil, which were isolated and fully characterized from C. elegans. Adenosine is known as an antiarrhythmic drug, and is found commercially as Adenocard . The identified metabolites were investigated for their wound healing efficiency against pigs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the comprehensive series of isolated alkaloids derived from Cunninghamella sp., and future research may reveal new bioactive molecules.

passages.text: Compared to the isolated alkaloids from Cunninghamella, biotransformation has become the leading strategy for producing several compounds that have significant biodiversity. For example, Chalom et al. reported on the oxidative transformation of stemofoline during fermentation with C. elegans TISTR. The study resulted in three bioactive alkaloid derivatives (shown in Fig. 5) that displayed potential inhibition against acetylcholinesterase with (IC50 = 11.01 +- 1.49 mM) compared to the precursor (IC50 = 45.1 +- 5.46 mM). Lu et al. have also investigated the biotransformation of vermitaline via C. echinulata (ACCC 30369), producing new alkaloid derivatives that were characterized by NMR and mass spectra. The biotransformed compounds were identified as 7alpha-hydroxyvermitaline-7-O-beta-d-galactofuranoside, 7alpha-hydroxyrubijervine-7-O-beta-d-galactofuranoside, and 7alpha-hydroxyrubijervine, 7alpha-hydroxyvermitaline, as shown in Fig. 6.
Oxidation and hydroxylation biotransformation of stemofoline alkaloids through fermentation by Cunninghamella elegans TIST 3370.
New alkaloid derivatives being transformed from verminaline by Cunninghamella echinulata.

Based on the literature, it was clearly noted that until now, few reports have discussed the isolation and biotransformation of alkaloids by Cunninghamella sp., despite their potential efficacy in drugs (Table 2). A huge gap is still being observed between Cunninghamella-derived alkaloids compared to the estimated number of plant-derived alkaloids represented by <60% of all potential drugs. Hence, further investigations regarding Cunninghamella-derived alkaloids are highly recommended, which could be a fruitful source for new bioactive agents for efficient drugs.

Fatty acids

Several Cunninghamella sp., like C. elegans, C. echinulata and C. bainieri, have shown a potential affinity toward the fabrication of a plethora of lipid compounds. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) can be accumulated in significant quantities by Cunninghamella, such as gamma-linoleic acid (GLA). Different chromatographic and spectroscopic methods were used to determine the PUFA profile of various Cunninghamella sp. One of the main PUFA in Cunninghamella is GLA, which represents 21.7% and 21.1% of the total lipid content in C. echinulata and C. blakesleeana, respectively. GLA plays a crucial role in brain function and normal growth with developments. An additional investigation recently analyzed the fatty acid (FA) contents in C. echinulata using GC-MS. Experimentally, the chemical profile analysis demonstrated the variation percentages of several FAs; saturated FAs comprised 44.49%, monounsaturated FAs comprised 19.91%, and PUFAs comprised 35.61%. Linoleic acid recorded the highest value at 13.79%, followed by stearic (12.78%) and then oleic acid (12.50%), while GLA yielded a suitable percent (8.02%). Additional types of PUFAs appeared, including eicosapentaenoic acid, arachidonic acid, and docosahexaenoic acid. The production yield of FAs could be increased through optimization of the cultivation conditions. A comparative study after several trials revealed that lipids (1.43 g L-1) could be accumulated in Cunninghamella sp. under the conditions of 5 g peptone and 20 g sucrose for 9 days. Under the optimum conditions after 6 days, the majority of the produced FA was saturated. Meanwhile, the PUFAs were the minor component, including palmitic acid, followed by oleic acid and GLA. In contrast, the FA profile was wholly changed under different conditions (9 days, followed by 3 days at 15  C) such that oleic acid was predominant with increasing percent of GLA from 1.14 to 3.22%.

In the continued search for isolated FAs from Cunninghamella sp., Salicorn 5 was also employed in the isolation of a number of PUFAs, like linoleic acid, GLA, oleic acid and other lipids. Although the amount of lipids produced by Salicorn 5 (Cunninghamella sp.) was relatively small compared to those formed in vegetables (e.g., rapeseed oil at 35-40%), the short generation time and high growth rate of fungi make their continued investigation worthwhile. Additional reports have investigated the isolation and identification of stearic, palmitic and oleic acids from C. blakesleeana and C. elegans extracts using column chromatography. Gas chromatography (GC) was also successfully employed for the characterization of several FAs in various quantities from C. blakesleeana biomass. The major FA was stearic acid (74.61%), followed by palmitic acid (10.35%), whereas the lowest percent was characterized by arachidic acid. Consequently, based on the relevant results, Cunninghamella sp. could be used as a commercial source for these types of secondary metabolites.

An in-depth investigation showed that Cunninghamella is superior in the isolation of several FAs, while the biotransformed compounds associated with this class have yet to be reported. Finally, it is worth mentioning that essential FAs cannot be synthesized by humans, and it must be obtained from diets. Analysis of the FA composition showed that PUFAs represented 87.03% of the total FAs, comprising oleic acid (35.57%), linoleic acid (21.58%), palmitoleic acid (16.31%), and linolenic acid (13.28%), while eicosenoic acid, stearic acid, myristic acid, and arachidic acid were found in much lower amounts. A relevant investigation revealed that the lipid compositions were comparable to those of the edible oils and fats; hence, Cunninghamella sp. could be successfully applied as an important source of edible oils.
Steroids

Steroids have emerged in living organisms with diverse and potential activity. Phytosterol compounds were reported from various Cunninghamella sp., including beta-sitosterol and alpha-amyrin from C. elegans and C. blakesleeana, in addition to stigmasterol from Cunninghamella sp. In general, these compounds are commonly known in the plant kingdom as having a wide range of medical purposes. For instance, the leaves of Odontonema strictum are rich in beta-sitosterol and stigmasterol valued at 60% and 40%, respectively.alpha-Amyrin has emerged in several plant species with potential activities (e.g., anti-inflammatory, antitumor, hepatoprotective and anxiolytic). However, the accurate determination of this compound in plant sources is still limited due to problems associated with efficient isolation, identification and quantification. Besides that, the isolation of such compounds for examination against diseases has not been specifically established. As a result, Cunninghamella could be an alternative source for such compounds and a suitable candidate for discovering new bioactive agents. In addition, a previous study has reported that ergosterol, stigmasta-7,22-diene-3beta,5alpha,6alpha-triol and stigmasterol have been isolated from Salicorn 5 (Cunninghamella sp.). These compounds were also produced from halophyte Salicornia bigelovii, explaining that endophytic fungi have a potential affinity to create the same chemical compounds or comparable ones produced by their hosts.

Conversely, biotransformation action plays a vital role in revealing the biodiversity in steroid production by Cunninghamella (Table 3). For instance, C. echinulata was involved in the isolation of ergosterol, besides two novel adipate esters from fusidic acid. The species was also used in a formylation reaction to obtain a unique fusidic acid derivative identified as 3-O-formyl-27-hydroxyfusidic acid. The chemical structures were elucidated by intensive spectroscopic methods like 1D, 2D-NMR and HRESIMS. In silico studies induced a significant agonist/antagonist effect through binding to the mu opioid receptor and antidiabetic activity via aldose reductase inhibitory action. It was observed that fusidic acid in mammals can be metabolized via C-3 or C-27 oxidation and glucuronide conjugation. Compared to mammals, microbes used C-3 and C-6 oxidation, C-6 and C-7 hydroxylation, and deacetylation of C-16, and then spontaneous lactone formation. Interestingly, modification on the side chain of fusidic acid rarely occurred. However, among several organisms, C. echinulata was the most efficient fungi in biotransformation, causing oxidation successfully at C-26 and C-27. Furthermore, a number of bioactive stereoselective derivatives were created such as fermentation of mesterolone by C. blakesleeana, producing a number of stereoselective steroids (as shown in Fig. 7a), which were investigated against different activities like anticancer, phosphodiesterase-5 enzymes, and oxidative burst. Moreover, three additional new steroids were obtained from the biotransformed androgenic steroid mibolerone with C. blakesleeana and C. echinulata.Cunninghamella sp. showed high capacity to catalyze the hydroxylation at the allylic positions of C-1, C-6, C-10, C-11, and C-20. C-6, C-10, and C-11 were the sites for beta-hydroxylation, whereas alpha-hydroxylation occurred at C-1, as shown in Fig. 7b. The produced compounds were investigated against different activities, including beta-glucuronidase inhibitory, anticancer and leishmanicidal activity. By the same way, mestanolone was also hydroxylated and transformed by C. blakesleeana to afford new steroidal derivatives, as shown in Fig. 7b. A number of steroidal derivatives were fabricated via microbial transformation of etonogestrel utilizing C. echinulata and C. blakesleeana, which showed cytotoxic activity. The transformed molecules were biosynthesized through epoxidation and hydroxylation at C-6, C-10, and C-15, whereas the epoxy ring was formed between the C-11 and C-22 positions (Fig. 8). Moreover, the biotransformation of adrenosterone and cortexolone resulted in the production of new derivatives with C. elegans via hydroxylation, as presented in Fig. 8. Notably, from the relevant and aforementioned studies, it was observed that steroidal biotransformation basically occurred via hydroxylation at different positions of the steroid skeleton.

Polysaccharides, polyphenols and quinones

Cunninghamella is thought to be a possible source for polysaccharides (Fig. 9) like chitosan, which can be recovered in significant amounts from fungal cell walls. Chitosan is also produced from other fungal sources, like Rhizopus arrhizus, Mucor rouxii, Aspergillus niger, Penicillium notatum and Absidia orchidis. Fungal chitosan is preferred over animal chitosan because the latter builds up in the renal tissue and increases the excretion of calcium in urine, which might result in kidney stone formation. Using three in vitro tests, fungal oligochitosan isolated from C. elegans was shown to exhibit more potent antioxidant activity than animal chitosan (reducing power, hydroxyl radical chelation and iron chelation) with a total antioxidant capacity of 17%, 40% and 13%, respectively. However, animal chitosan showed no activity in these tests. Gallic acid (GA) was also isolated from C. elegans, which induced a variety of biological activity to be described later.
Secondary metabolites isolated from the Cunninghamella species.

Another Cunninghamella metabolite, ubiquinone, was used as a biochemical marker for the classification and identification of Cunninghamella sp. This methodology helps with morphological taxonomy to tackle a number of issues pertaining to classification and phylogenetics. Cunninghamella has three types of ubiquinones based on the carbon numbers in their side chain (ubiquinone Q6, Q9 and Q10), as presented in Fig. 9. Ubiquinone Q6 was found in C. bertholletie, C. elegans and C. ramosa, while ubiquinone Q9 was found in C. elegans, C. blakesleeana and C. echinulata. However, C. bertholletie and C. elegans are the only producers of ubiquinone Q10. On the other hand, it is worth noting that the bio-transformed compounds are still missing, and further investigations are required.
Biological, agricultural, environmental, and industrial applications

The secondary metabolites fabricated by endophytic fungi are well defined by their vital role in several applications. As the global population increases, the request for pharmaceutical and agricultural substances has dramatically increased. Hence, Cunninghamella sp. will gain tremendous attention in the future, particularly for the isolation of bioactive compounds. The current section will discuss the various biological, industrial, agricultural, and environmental values of previously isolated metabolites, and provide new insights into the recent applications of Cunninghamella sp. and as summarized in Table 4 and Fig. 10.

Biomedical uses of the chemically identified compounds derived from Cunninghamella species.
Biological activities

Fungal secondary metabolites are of intense interest due to their considerable biological activities. A strong relationship has been created between the pharmaceutical and biochemical industries with endophytic fungi, in particular Cunninghamella, due to the abundance of several promising metabolites that have various biological values, like anti-cancer, antioxidants, antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial values (Table 4). These values offer significant potential for their usage in medicine.
Antimicrobial activity

Cunninghamella sp. has become a focal point of interest as one of the principal sources for the biodiversity of secondary metabolites used as antimicrobial agents. A number of relevant studies have investigated the antimicrobial activity of the isolated compounds with an emphasis on fatty acids. For instance, GLA stands out among the fatty acids due to its wide range of biological activities, which include its ability to fight off a variety of Gram-negative periodontal pathogens, particularly Prevotella intermedia and Porphyromonas gingivalis, when triclosan (a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent found in toothpaste) is used as a positive control. The study revealed that GLA was more potent against the tested pathogens with a minimum inhibition concentration (MIC) of 39.06 and 9.76 mug mL-1, respectively, compared to triclosan (1250 and 78.12 mug mL-1, respectively) against the same pathogens. GLA was also shown to be active against several oral pathogens like Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Candida albicans, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and Streptococcus mutans. In addition, another study has reported on the antimicrobial activity of isolated fatty acids against Staphylococcus aureus, Pencillium expansum and Salmonella typhimurium. The results showed that stearic acid was the most potent compound against S. aureus with a zone of inhibition of 15 +- 0.5 mm at MIC of 360 mug mL-1, compared to palmitic acid and oleic acid (13.0 +- 0.1 and 11.0 +- 0.3 mm, respectively). Palmitic acid and oleic acid showed significant antimicrobial efficacy against S. typhimurium and P. expansum with a zone of inhibition of 8 +- 0.8 and 8.5 +- 0.6 mm at MIC of 690 and 660 mug mL-1, respectively, compared with stearic acid with the use of gentamycin, ampicillin, and amphotericin B as standard antimicrobial drugs, as introduced in Table 4. Furthermore, chitosan isolated from C. elegans showed antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli, S. aureus and C. albicans with zones of inhibition of 33.8, 38.2 and 23.5 mm at MIC of 0.57, 0.37 and 1.25 mg mL-1, respectively. Oral administration of an ethanol extract of Cunninghamella sp. (400 mg kg-1) resulted in potential safety for up to 5000 mg kg-1, and no problems appeared in the kidney or liver functions. In the same context, an alcoholic extract of C. elegans induced activation against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, while an ethyl acetate extract showed the highest efficacy against S. aureus, followed by an ether extract with an inhibition zone at 29.2 +- 0.08 and 26.2 +- 0.08 mm, respectively. The lowest activity was obtained by a butanol extract (2.4 +- 0.1 mm), followed by an ethyl acetate extract (3.4 +- 0.5) against Streptococcus pyogenes.

Adenosine was evaluated for its antimicrobial activity, and the results indicated that adenosine was most active against S. aureus with an inhibition zone of 30 +- 0.1 mm at a concentration of 20 mug mL-1 compared to those of streptomycin and penicillin G as standard antibiotics (25 +- 0.2 and 29.5 +- 0.8 mm, respectively). Additionally, the topical application of 1 mg mL-1 adenosine to an experimentally excised wound surface sped up the healing process, according to a study on the wound-healing properties of adenosine isolated from C. elegans. Topical application of adenosine showed 76.5% wound correction after 14 days since treatment started, which was close to that of the standard drug latmoxef (100%). Complete wound correction by adenosine occurred after 18 days.

Moreover, glucose esters of different fatty acids from C. echinulata were synthesized using lipases as biocatalysts. The biological activity assay of glucose fatty acid esters from C. echinulata indicated that they were efficient against Bacillus subtilis, Candida albicans, and Staphylococcus aureus at MIC 40 mug mL-1 with inhibition zones of 14.1, 14.3 and 12.3 mm, respectively. The results revealed the high pathogenic activity of fatty acid esters present in Cunninghamella sp. compared to those founded in U. isabelline. This could be attributed to GLA present in the lipids of C. echinulata, which has been recognized for its antibacterial activity in higher amounts. Furthermore, the glucose fatty acid esters from C. echinulata demonstrated notable insecticidal action against Aedes aegypti larvae with LC50 of 0.54 mg L-1. Additionally, after treatment with 10 g mL-1 of glucose esters, the SKOV-3 ovarian cancer cell line experienced a high proportion of apoptosis (39.2%). Furthermore, beta-sitosterol exhibits potent antiviral activity against the influenza A virus. A study by Shokry et al. showed that beta-sitosterol demonstrated promising antiviral efficacy against A/H1N1 and A/H5N1 strains with IC50 of 0.975 and 0.295 mug mL-1, respectively, compared to zanamivir as a positive control. It has been discovered that beta-sitosterol can influence various viral replication processes, including viral adsorption and replication. The significant inhibitory impact of beta-sitosterol against the hemagglutinin surface protein and neuraminidase, with docking energies of -6.40 and -29.40 kcal mol-1, was attributed as the mechanism of beta-sitosterol's antiviral activity.

The antiparasitic efficacy of alpha-amyrin was in vitro testing against Trypanosoma cruzi. The study showed that the isolated compound was more effective against the amastigote stage than the trypomastigote stage with an IC50 value of 9.08 mug mL-1 compared to that of the reference medication nifurtimox (3.07 mug mL-1). A molecular docking study indicated that alpha-amyrin has a greater affinity to T. cruzi cysteine synthase (TcCS) with a binding energy of -9.8 kcal mol-1.

In conclusion, from the tabulated data (Table 4), it was clearly observed that most of the antimicrobial research involved very few species of Cunninghamella, e.g., C. elegans, C. echinulata and C. blakesleeana. In addition, fatty acids exhibited the highest antimicrobial activity compared to other classes. This is consistent with previous literature data, which confirmed the potential antimicrobial activity of fatty acids. However, further investigations are recommended with the incorporation of new active species of Cunninghamella, aiming to isolate new lead compounds.
Anticancer

GLA has demonstrated anticancer activity in patients with breast cancer. Due to its capacity to lower estrogen receptor expression and enhance the inhibitory effects of tamoxifen through enhanced downregulation of estrogen receptor-mediated growth, it has been demonstrated that GLA (at a dose of 2.8 g per day) can be used as an adjunct to primary tamoxifen (at a dose of 20 mg per day) in cases of endocrine-sensitive breast cancer. Occasionally, some of the patients would not have the ability for natural GLA production, and this would lead to using GLA dietary supplements. The high productivity of GLA was enhanced in C. echinulata that had been treated with a pulsed strong magnetic field via physical mutagenesis technology. Yields of GLA (Mut-29, Mut-15, Mut-64) were improved by 46.2%, 23.1%, and 19.2%, respectively, compared to the parent strain. On the other hand, GLA was successfully incorporated in fatty acid lithium salt to increase its solubility. Consequently, it could be smoothly administrated to the cell. It was found that using lithium gamma-linolenate enhanced the permeability of cancer agents and improved the cytotoxic activity of GLA. Two dosage levels were used (either 0.84 g kg-1 (n = 1) or 0.28 g kg-1 (n = 2)) with the oral treatment of one dose value of a total of 10.5 g per patient (n = 2). When compared with conventional regimens, treatment with GLA indicated the survival of pancreatic cancer patients that showed a potential result.

To maximize the impact of the anticancer efficacy in Cunninghamella sp., a phenolic acid such as gallic acid (GA) was previously isolated from C. elegans. Gallic acid has a wide variety of biological activities. Recently, GA has shown strong cytotoxic effects on colon cancer cell lines. Three different types of cell lines, representing various stages of cancer severity, were used to assess GA's cytotoxic effect: colon epithelial cells CRL1790, which represent the non-tumorigenic stage; and colorectal cancer cell lines SW480 and SW620, which represent the primary tumor stage and the aggressive metastatic stage, respectively. The results revealed that GA inhibited the cell growth of SW480 and SW 620 at IC50 of 22.39 +- 2.12 and 11.8 +- 1.5 muM, respectively. Furthermore, GA showed high selectivity toward cancer cells rather than non-cancer cells due to the high IC50 (>100 muM) of GA against CRL1790 cells. Moreover, the results of the cell cycle analysis of the tested cell lines showed that GA induced prominent S and G2/M phases. GA changed the frequency of the cells from 34.2% to 43.8% at the S phase, and 7.7% to 14.5% at the G2/M phase. These results indicate that GA may affect DNA replication, inducing cell cycle arrest in the S and G2/M stages. These findings were supported by an in vivo experimental model, and immunofluorescent analysis of the tumor tissues taken from sacrificed mice showed that GA had a downregulating effect on several G-Quadruplexes (G4)-enriched oncogenes, leading to DNA damage.
